2. On regolith particle evolution processes:
In paragraph [20], the authors note that impact gardening, thermal cycling, and solar wind
irradiation contribute to fragmentation and abrasion. However, the role of agglomeration
processes is not discussed. For example, breccia particles may be formed by the strong
12
compression due to meteoroid impact, and agglutinate particles are formed by the gathering of
partly melted fragments. Also, fragmentation and abrasion can have opposing effects on
particle morphology. Such processes must be considered to accurately evaluate regolith
evolution. The current interpretation risks oversimplifying the particle evolution process.
Response: Very insightful comment. We fully agree that our initial version of Figure 5 and the
associated discussion in paragraph [20] oversimplified the mechanisms underlying
morphological equilibrium, as we did not adequately address the role of impact agglutination,
nor did we provide sufficient discussion of the contrasting effects of fragmentation and
abrasion. As the reviewer correctly notes, agglutination plays a critical role in the formation of
breccias and agglutinates, while fragmentation and abrasion may exert opposing influences on
particle morphology. The omission of these aspects in our initial submission indeed made our
conceptual model less comprehensive.
In the revised manuscript, we have restructured our discussion of morphological saturation
mechanisms to provide a more complete representation of lunar surface processes. Specifically,
particle reshaping mechanisms now include the following.
 Impact gardening (mainly abrasion caused by repeated interactions among numerous
grains within the regolith)
 Impact fragmentation (grain breakage via direct energy deposition during impacts)
 Impact agglutination (fusion of surrounding grains into breccias or agglutinates due to
impact-induced melts or semi-plastic phases)
 Impact sputtering (deposits from impact events appearing randomly on the surface of
minerals, forming a sputtering deposit layer that modifies particle morphology)
 Impact abrasion (localized surface wear caused by micrometeoroid strikes or secondary
impacts that generate linear scratches)
 Thermal fatigue (fracturing and disintegration from diurnal thermal stresses)
 Solar wind irradiation (implantation of high-energy ions producing lattice defects, which
increase susceptibility to subsequent weathering-induced reshaping; in addition, sputtering
by the solar wind which may also erode particle surfaces)
Among these processes, impact agglutination is particularly distinctive as it transforms
“simple particles” into “complex particles” in a cumulative manner, producing irregular
aggregates that strongly affect overall regolith morphology. Other processes generally reshape
particles without altering their fundamental type, although “complex particles” may shed small
fragments that revert to “simple particles”. Both particle types are subsequently subject to
further modification by the full suite of processes.
Regarding the relative influence of fragmentation and abrasion, previous studies
demonstrate that surface exposure age correlates with the grain size of lunar regolith in the >1
mm fraction (Morris et al., 1976; McKay et al., 1974), but this relationship weakens below the
centimetre scale. Furthermore, Weibull statistics show that smaller grains require
disproportionately higher stresses to fail completely (Weibull, 1951; McDowell et al., 2000).
This result implies that for lunar regolith dominated by <1 mm particles, impact fragmentation
is limited, and the majority of impact energy is redistributed into broad-scale impact gardening,
which thus emerges as the primary driver of morphological modification.
Despite marked differences in age, geological setting, basaltic source regions,
micrometeorite flux, and solar wind exposure between CE5 and CE6 sites, the morphometrics
of corresponding particle types remain remarkably consistent. This convergence strongly
suggests that long-term particle reshaping, governed primarily by impact gardening with
contributions from agglutination, drives both “simple” and “complex” particles toward stable
morphologies, such that additional space weathering exerts only minor influence on particle
morphometrics (Reply Figure 5).

4. On the Interpretation of Agglutinate Porosity Differences:
The discussion in paragraphs [18] and [19] are largely speculative. Paragraph [18] explains the
lower internal porosity observed in CE6 agglutinates from the different micrometeorite
bombardment condition in nearside and farside. This can be proved by comparing with the data

contents, and gas escape efficiency is mentioned, but the argument lacks cohesion and empirical support. These sections would benefit from a clearer presentation and more cautious language regarding the proposed mechanisms.
Response: Thanks for this insightful comment. In paragraph [18], we noted that previous
research has shown CE5 soils experienced relatively lower temperatures as induced by
micrometeorite impacts compared to Apollo soils (Nie et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2022). In
contrast, silicon isotope modeling suggests that for CE6 soils, the impact-induced glass
formation temperatures—primarily controlled by micrometeorite impact velocities—are likely
comparable to those documented for Apollo soils (Zhang et al., 2025a). We hypothesized that
the higher glass formation temperatures associated with more intense micrometeorite
bombardment at the CE6 landing site may have contributed to the lower agglutinate void ratios
observed in CE6 relative to CE5.
The reviewer’s suggestion to verify this hypothesis using Apollo data is particularly
valuable. Since our CE5–CE6 comparison already uses Apollo soils as a benchmark, Apollo
samples provide an excellent reference dataset for agglutinate porosity. We selected an Apollo
17 sample (73002) for this comparison because this site is incorporated in the thermal modeling
of Nie et al. (2024). Following the same analytical procedures described in response to
Fig. 6a–b) and calculated their void ratios using the same methodology as for CE5 and CE6.
The resulting average void ratio for Apollo 17 agglutinates (e = 0.10) is nearly identical to

Finally, regarding paragraphs [18–19], we agree with the reviewer that the original
discussion linking agglutinate structure, volatile contents, and gas escape efficiency lacked
coherence and empirical support. We have substantially revised this section to present a
mechanism-based, but non-exclusive, interpretation.
In silicate melts, lower viscosity—typically at higher temperatures—facilitates bubble
ascent, coalescence, and the development of permeable vesicle networks, allowing for efficient
open-system degassing once pathways connect to the atmospheric vacuum (Harris et al., 2008;
Gonnermann & Manga, 2013). In micrometeorite-formed agglutinates, transient melt films can
enable gases to vent through connected vesicles before cooling; when degassing is efficient,
the resulting internal porosity can be significantly reduced compared to less-degassed clasts
(Rust et al., 2004).
We now interpret the lower porosity of CE6 agglutinates as consistent with (rather than
proving) more efficient syn-formation gas escape under open-system conditions. At the same
time, we explicitly acknowledge alternative explanations, including viscosity contrasts during
18
formation, variations in melt fraction, vesicle connectivity, and post-formation vesicle collapse.
We also clarify that we do not directly measure volatile contents in this study; our inference is
textural and mechanistic, supported by established degassing literature. These clarifications
have been incorporated into the revised manuscript, with appropriately cautious language.

Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for pointing out this important issue. We
acknowledge that in the original version we did not clearly explain the basis for subdividing
lunar regolith into “lunar dust,” “bulk soil,” and “large particles.” The definition of “lunar dust”
follows the commonly adopted convention that classifies particles’ equivalent diameter smaller
than 20 μm (Sun et al., 2017; Wallace et al., 2009). Although this fraction is an essential
component of the regolith, its extremely small size makes large-scale morphological analysis
difficult. In this study, therefore, we treat this group primarily as the end-product of space
weathering.
For the “large particles” fraction, we establish a threshold based on the relatively low
volume percentage of particles’ equivalent diameter >200 μm in the CE5 and CE6 soils. As
shown in Reply Figure 1, such particles account for <15% of the total regolith volume. Within
the bulk soil micro-CT framework adopted in this study, this fraction yields only a limited
number of measurable particles, making robust statistical analysis of their morphology
challenging. Nonetheless, this does not imply that large particles are excluded from the
saturation in morphological modification of space weathering, as we further discuss in response
to Comment #28-29.
By contrast, the 20–200 μm fraction constitutes the dominant component of the CE5 and
CE6 soils, accounting for >60% of the total volume. This size range therefore represents the
main carrier of surface-evolutionary signatures and is the primary focus of our analysis, which
we refer to as the “bulk soil fraction.”

Response: Thanks for this valuable recommendation. We have incorporated both references
and briefly summarize their key contributions to grain-scale morphological transformations
under space weathering. Keller & McKay (1997) used TEM to show that most lunar soil
particles develop nanometer-scale surface rims (typically ~60–200 nm) that fall into four end-
member types: amorphous (solar-wind irradiation damage with preferential cation sputtering),
inclusion-rich (impact-vapor–deposited, containing abundant npFe0), multiple (irradiation
layer overlain by vapor-deposited material), and vesicular (abundant <50 nm vesicles from
evolved implanted gases following pulse heating). These rims, and especially npFe0,
systematically modify surface texture and optical/magnetic properties, directly linking
microstructure to macroscopic “maturity” signals.
Noble et al. (2016) characterized natural micrometeoroid microcraters on lunar grains and
documented melt linings (~0.5–2 µm), recrystallized layers, extensive shock-damaged zones
extending up to tens of micrometers, near-surface vesiculation, annealing of solar-flare tracks,
and pervasive npFe0 (~3–7 nm) in melt/recrystallized layers, demonstrating how localized
melting, vapor deposition, and shock collectively reshape grain surfaces and rims at the
nanoscale.

answer. Also, it would be good to succinctly state your hypothesis here.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this constructive guidance. In the revised Introduction,
we clarify the connections between mineralogy, space weathering, impact processes, and
resulting particle shape, and we support these links with additional references. Variations in
primary lava composition yield distinct mineralogical assemblages in lunar regolith, which in
turn govern particle-scale mechanical responses to impact processes. For example, plagioclase
is more prone to brittle fracture than pyroxene, rendering plagioclase-rich basalts and breccias
more susceptible to crack propagation and localized abrasion during meteoroid bombardment
(Hörz et al., 1984; Taylor et al., 2001). At the microscale, individual mineral phases respond
differently to space weathering processes such as solar-wind implantation, localized melting,
and vaporization, further altering particle morphology (Denevi et al., 2023; Cao et al., 2025).
In addition, spatial variations in impact energy across the lunar surface drive differences in
lithologic fragmentation and regolith gardening, both of which significantly influence particle
shape (Papike et al., 1982). Taken together, we emphasize that regolith particle morphology
encodes an integrated signature of local geological context and cumulative space weathering
modification.

maintain a coherent narrative, we also now state our working hypothesis succinctly at the end

and evidential basis of the study.

According to Head et al. (2020), mare basalt protolith types include: solidified

Response: Very valuable comment. We agree that in our initial discussion we overstated the role of fragmentation in shaping particle morphologies within the bulk soil fraction, and we now recognize that the dominant regime in this size range is better described by a combination of mixing and agglutinate production.
In the revised manuscript, we have reorganized our discussion of particle reshaping mechanisms to capture the full spectrum of processes acting on lunar regolith. Specifically, include the following.
 Impact gardening (including mixing; primarily abrasion caused by repeated interactions among numerous grains within the regolith matrix)
 Impact fragmentation (grain breakage via direct energy deposition during impacts);
 Impact agglutination (fusion of surrounding grains into breccias or agglutinates due to impact-induced melts or semi-plastic phases)
 Impact sputtering (deposits from impact events appearing randomly on the surface of minerals, forming a sputtering deposit layer that modifies particle morphology)
 Impact abrasion (localized surface wear caused by micrometeoroid strikes or secondary impacts that generate linear scratches)
 Thermal fatigue (fracturing and disintegration from diurnal thermal stresses)
 Solar wind irradiation (implantation of high-energy ions producing lattice defects, which increase susceptibility to subsequent weathering-induced reshaping; in addition, sputtering by the solar wind which may also erode particle surfaces)
Among these, impact agglutination is particularly distinctive as it transforms “simple particles” into “complex particles” in a cumulative fashion, generating irregular aggregates that strongly influence bulk regolith morphology. By contrast, other processes reshape particles without fundamentally altering their type, although “complex particles” may shed small fragments that revert to “simple particles.” Both particle classes are then subject to additional modification by the full suite of processes.
Regarding the relative influence of fragmentation and abrasion, previous studies demonstrate that surface exposure age correlates with the grain size of lunar regolith in the >1 mm fraction (Morris, 1976; McKay et al., 1974), but this correlation weakens at <1 mm. Furthermore, Weibull fracture statistics demonstrate that smaller grains require higher stresses to fail completely (Weibull, 1951; McDowell et al., 2000). Thus, for the <1 mm grains that dominate the lunar regolith, impact fragmentation likely contributes only minimally to reshaping, and most of the impact energy is redistributed into broad-scale impact gardening, which thus emerges as the dominant driver of morphological modification (Reply Figure 6).
Despite clear differences in age, geological setting, basalt provenance, micrometeoroid flux, and solar wind irradiation between the CE5 and CE6 sampling sites, the morphometrics of corresponding particle types remain remarkably consistent. This convergence strongly suggests that long-term particle reshaping, governed primarily by impact gardening with contributions from agglutination, has driven both simple and complex particles toward stable morphologies, such that additional weathering exerts only a minor influence on their morphometrics.
Finally, we also fully agree with the reviewer that a more robust assessment of regolith maturity requires integrating multiple indicators. Accordingly, we now describe space weathering intensity using a multi-proxy suite of maturity parameters, including agglutinate abundance, Is/FeO values, and regolith surface exposure ages. For example, CE5 soils contain ~8% agglutinates, exhibit an Is/FeO value of ~14, and an exposure age of ~1.5 Ma (Qian et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025), whereas CE6 soils contain ~17% agglutinates, exhibit an Is/FeO value of ~56.5, and an exposure age of ~2.1 Ma (Zhang et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025). These parameters collectively indicate that CE6 experienced stronger space weathering than CE5. The consistent morphometrics observed across both soils therefore imply that even the less weathered CE5 regolith had already reached morphological saturation by its exposure age of ~1.5 Ma. This conclusion is further supported by our comparison with Apollo 17 sample 73002 (see Response to Comment #29), which represents an even more mature regolith yet exhibits similarly stable morphologies.

Figure 5 has been revised accordingly to illustrate the interplay among agglutination, fragmentation, and abrasion.

Response: Thanks for this valuable comment. We acknowledge that paragraph [15] in the original manuscript contained several shortcomings. First, our initial references to Apollo 11 and Apollo 17 soils did not specify sampling locations, which could have led to misunderstanding. Second, as Reviewer #1 correctly notes, the use of fine particle content as an indicator of space weathering intensity is problematic. Inspired by this (see Response to Comment 1(1)), we revisited the literature and found that local factors, such as proximity to boulders or recent craters, exert a strong influence on grain size characteristics (King, 1977). Thus, fine particle content cannot reliably serve as a proxy for space weathering intensity. In response, we have revised paragraph [15] to focus instead on a comprehensive description of space weathering intensity in CE5 and CE6 soils (see Revision to Comment #28).
And as this reviewer (#2) further suggests, validation of the morphological saturation effect requires more specific comparison with Apollo soils. To this end, we have incorporated data from the Apollo 17 double-drive tube sample 73001/2, specifically the upper 20 cm section (73002). This sample, recovered from the Light Mantle landslide deposit at the base of the South Massif in Taurus–Littrow Valley, was opened and scanned by micro-CT in 2019, with data subsequently released (Eckley et al., 2025). Previous work indicates that 73002 sampled multiple basalt flows, and its maturity is well constrained: the uppermost regolith exhibits an Is/FeO value of ~74 (Morris et al., 2022) and a surface exposure age of ~3.0 Ma (McFadden et al., 2024). By comparison, CE5 soils have an Is/FeO value of ~14 and an exposure age of ~1.5 Ma (Qian et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025), while CE6 soils show an Is/FeO of ~56.5 and an exposure age of ~2.1 Ma (Zhang et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025). Thus, the Apollo 17 sample is more mature than both CE5 and CE6, and its derivation from a landslide deposit ensures mineralogical and lithological complexity. If morphological saturation is also observed in 73002, this would imply that such saturation can be achieved by the relatively short exposure age of CE5 (~1.5 Ma).
It should be noted, however, that the Apollo 73002 CT radiographs were acquired at a resolution of 25.8 μm (Eckley et al., 2025; Reply Fig. 7a), which limits morphological characterization to particles larger than ~500 μm. This precludes direct comparison with the bulk soil fraction (20–200 μm) analyzed in this study. To enable robust comparison, we therefore selected basalt particles in the 500–700 μm range from both CE5 and CE6 soils, using basalt as the common material for analysis (see Response to Reviewer#1 Comment 1(2)).
For CE5 and CE6, which are shallow scoop samples with relatively few large particles, we manually selected ~200 particles for each, from which we obtained 22 basalts from CE5 and 27 from CE6. For Apollo 73002, we restricted our analysis to the uppermost ~3 cm of regolith (to align with the near-surface context of CE5 and CE6 and to ensure comparable space weathering intensity). Basalt grains were readily identified from radiographs (Reply Fig. 7b), manually extracted, and reconstructed in 3D (Reply Fig. 7c–d). The larger sample size of Apollo 73002 allowed us to extract 110 basalt grains, ensuring statistical robustness.
Our morphometric results (Reply Fig. 7e–h) show highly similar distributions of AR, S, Cx, and R across basalts from CE5, CE6, and Apollo 17 (73002). The mean values differ by <10%, with comparable standard deviations. These results indicate that morphological saturation is likely already established by the CE5 surface exposure age of ~1.5 Ma, although larger CE5 and CE6 datasets will be necessary to further test this conclusion in the future.

Response: We thank the reviewer for this valuable comment. We acknowledge that our
manuscript did not originally address the latitudinal and longitudinal influence on
micrometeoroid flux. After carefully reviewing Sim et al. (2017), we note that micrometeoroid
flux is indeed latitude-dependent. This observation is consistent with the lunar surface flux
model of Jeong et al. (2015), which shows reduced flux at higher latitudes but remains
symmetric with respect to latitude. Since the CE5 and CE6 sampling sites are located at
43.06°N and 41.625°S in opposite hemispheres, respectively, their latitudes are nearly identical
(as designed by orbital mission planning requirements), suggesting comparable fluxes under
the similar longitudinal conditions.
In theory, the nearside may experience partial shielding by the Earth, potentially resulting
in a higher flux on the farside. However, Cremonese et al. (2013) quantified the “Earth
shielding effect” and found it to be on the order of 10-3, which is negligible. Their model also

Response: Thanks for raising this important issue. We acknowledge that in the original version
our explanation of how gardening, thermal cycling, and solar wind irradiation contribute to
particle abrasion and fragmentation was not sufficiently clear, which may have led to confusion.
First, impact gardening is one of the dominant mechanisms reshaping lunar regolith
particles in our model (see Response to Comment #28-29). Within a given region, large
numbers of particles repeatedly make contact and undergo displacement, which results
predominantly in mechanical abrasion. (Tsuchiyama et al., 2022). For particles with structural
weaknesses—such as agglutinates containing abundant vesicles—gardening-induced
compression and stress concentration may also cause partial breakage.
Second, long-term thermal cycling, driven by daily non-uniform solar heating, induces
internal thermal stresses within particles. Over time, these stresses accumulate and may lead to
thermal fatigue, generating cracks that ultimately cause the particles to fracture (Ruesch et al.,
2020).
Finally, solar wind irradiation exerts its influence primarily in an indirect manner. The
implantation of high-energy ions generates crystalline defects that weaken lattice stability,
thereby making grains more susceptible to subsequent reshaping by other space weathering
processes (Maurette et al., 1975). In addition, sputtering by the solar wind which may also erode
particle surfaces (Tsuchiyama et al., 2022).
Together, these processes act in combination, progressively modifying particle
morphologies through abrasion and fragmentation.

fragmentation (grain breakage due to direct energy deposition during impacts90), impact
agglutination (where impact-induced melts or semi-plastic phases fuse surrounding grains into
agglutinates and breccias), impact sputtering (deposits from impact events appear randomly on
the surface of minerals, forming sputtering deposit layer that modify particle morphology46),
impact abrasion (localized surface wear induced by micrometeoroid impacts20,91 or secondary
impacts that generate linear scratches92), thermal fatigue (fracturing driven by thermal stresses
leading to ultimate grain disintegration90), and solar wind irradiation93 (high-energy ion
implantation generates crystalline defects, making grains more susceptible to subsequent space
weathering induced reshaping94; in addition, sputtering by solar wind may also erode particle
surfaces67).”

reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
We thank the authors for addressing our comments. From this, I see an immense improvement. This is demonstrated by a more robust literature review, which has helped guide the authors towards better interpretations of the data. However, there are still some outstanding clarifications and suggestions that I feel should be addressed before publication.
Paragraph 2:
According to the authors citations, the authors subdivisions for regolith particle sizes are based on simulant studies. How do these studies tie to natural regolith samples, other than their development to broadly mimic regolith composition? For example, the authors said that these divisions are based on different degrees of space weathering. Could the authors explain how these studies made this determination? I feel like a more robust description of this is warranted because to many researchers, anything <1 mm would be considered “dust” and described as “bulk soil”. If these classifications are the authors preference for the purposes of this work, I would make that clear in the text.
In addition, the observation of 20-200 um size fraction being more abundant than the “large” and “lunar dust” size fractions is in agreement with McKay et al 1974. It would be good to cite that here and elaborate why this phenomenon occurs when one would expect comminution to make smaller size fractions the most dominant.
Paragraph 5:
I would note here that regolith composition influences agglutinate abundance due to some mineral phases being more prone to melting. I recommend reviewing Adams and Charette, 1975: Chemical Fractionation of the Lunar Regolith by Impact Melting; Rhodes et al., 1975: Chemistry of Agglutinate Fractions in Lunar Soils.
Figure 2 appears to be blurry.
Supplementary Figure 2o: Nice work adding the extra data points. For stylistic purposes, each point is very similar in color, with Pyroxene and Olivene points being very close to the shaded region of Mp. Is it possible to change the color scheme of the figure so that the points for each mineral type are more easily distinguishable?
Paragraph 10:
Line 196-198: Solar wind contributes to npFe production embedded within agglutinates after exposure to kinetic energies associated from micrometeorite impacts. However, the glassy matrix is caused by impact melt, and solar wind is not a contributing factor. I would rephrase this to omit solar wind as an originating component to agglutinate formation and clarify that H from solar wind implantation into surface exposed regolith reduces iron in impact melt to form metallic iron nanoparticles (npFe) within agglutinitic glass. In addition, I would also elaborate on the proposed mechanisms that form vesicles within agglutinates.
Line 200-201: The phrasing of this sentence seems awkward. I recommend splitting these into two sentences, and introduce the influence of npFe when it is first introduced in the previous sentence.
I would also clarify what additional space weathering processes produce npFe, other than vapor deposition.
Paragraph 11:
Has the differences of vesicle morphology between glassy interiors and fragment interfaces been observed elsewhere using other methods?
Basu and McKay, 1985 conducted EDX analyses of the interfaces between agglutinitic melt and incorporated fragments and found no evidence of chemical gradation, suggesting that the two components don’t chemically influence each other. The authors results suggest that the interfaces influence vesicle morphology. Could the authors explain why this phenomenon occurs?
Additionally, do interfaces include older incorporated agglutinates? How can these agglutinate fragments be differentiated from lithic fragments in the authors CT data? How is this reconciled in the authors vesicle ratio calculations?
I am also curious how the authors define abundance of internal fragments. Is it a volumetric abundance? Numerical abundance? This is an important distinction as a particular Ir ratio may indicate one large fragment or multiple small fragments.
Paragraph 12:
I recommend removing the introduction of differences in micrometeorite bombardment and volatile mobilization as those are more relevant to the discussion.
The authors mention that the greater Ir values for bulk soils may be due to the inherent morphologies of fragmented larger agglutinates. Could it also be that bulk soil agglutinates form from smaller volumes of melt relative to the larger size fraction, and therefore would incorporate fewer fragments?
Paragraph 15:
Line 303-304: Agglutinate abundance is only a valid proxy for maturity for Is/FeO < 60. Agglutinate abundance saturates in more mature soils (Morris, 1976).
Line 306: I would say bombardment rather than vaporization, because npFe is found in melt AND vapor.
Line 307-310: Could the authors elaborate as to how regolith gardening manifests itself as exposure age? How is this age determined? The authors reference a paper that uses SEP tracks to identify exposure ages, however, for a given soil there ages can span millions of years while the average may only be only a fraction of the maximum age. The maximum age, therefore, may be a more appropriate metric to gauge the overall exposure age of a soil, since that is closer to the full duration that regolith had been exposed to space weathering processes. Are the ages the authors used for the Chang’e 5/6 samples the maximum age?
Paragraph 18
Please define “syn-formation”
Elaborate on transient temperatures. Do the authors mean diurnal heating? Would the authors suggested transient temperature realistically influence the temperatures which very quickly melt and quench regolith?
I am confused as to why the authors compare their results to 73002. Why would we expect this Apollo sample to be similar/different? The Apollo missions were largely equatorial and the Chang’e missions landed at much higher latitudes. If the transient temperature is micrometeorite flux or diurnal heating, which are latitudinally dependent, why is 73002 samples similar to the Chang’e 6 samples?
At the end of this paragraph the authors mention potential contributions to vesicle formation in agglutinates. The authors mention melt viscosity and cooling/welding history. These can be further elaborated on considering that melt compositions tend towards that of mafic compositions due to low melting temperatures of basaltic components and that the cooling history of agglutinitic melt is extremely fast (quenched).
Paragraph 19
Line 414-415: The authors mention that abrasion preferentially removes the fragments within agglutinates. How would this affect the Ir value if the vesicles are inherent to melt, not the fragments.
Do CE6 agglutinates generally contain more fragments? Why might this be the case?
Paragraph 20
Line 437-438: Generally, when correlating surface exposure proxies, be specific as to which ones. In this context, what exactly was grain size fraction compared to.
Paragraph 21
Line 452-454: I would specify that this saturation affects the bulk size fraction, as opposed to the entirety of the regolith (i.e. all size fractions).
73002 was found to be largely composed of highlands material with small amounts of basaltic material found throughout, mostly concentrated near the top 3 cm (Neuman et al., 2025: Revealing the Moon's Taurus‐Littrow Landslide via Integrated Analysis of Pristine Apollo 17 Soil Core 73001/2). I would clarify that 73002 is compositionally distinct from pure mare regolith and elaborate on this when making comparisons to Chang'e samples.
In Morris et al., 2022, they found that the in situ reworking zone of 73002 had an upper development age of ~17 Ma. The 3.0 Ma age found in SEP track densities was the average of exposure ages from individual particles in the core, and not reflective of the overall time regolith had been subject to regolith gardening. Therefore, it would be more appropriate to compare the maximum exposure ages of a soil to evaluate the saturation timescales of bulk soil morphology.

Response: Thanks for this very insightful and technically precise comment. We fully agree
that our previous justification for subdividing regolith particle sizes—based partly on simulant
studies—was not sufficiently rigorous and may not directly reflect the behavior of natural lunar
soils. After carefully re-evaluating our classification scheme, we acknowledge that (i) simulant-
based criteria cannot serve as primary evidence for subdivision, and (ii) our earlier statement
that the divisions correspond to “different degrees of space weathering” was not well supported
by the literature.
Our focus on lunar regolith fraction of particle size <1 mm arises from their well-established
importance in governing the space weathering properties of lunar soils (McKay et al., 1974).

agglutinate formation, three phases coexist: gas (volatiles), melt (impact-generated glass),

(i) Because agglutinates are mechanically weak (McKay et al., 1991), any older agglutinates
incorporated into a later generation of melt are likely to have undergone substantial
fragmentation during the impact event. Their characteristic vesicle networks and agglutinate
textures are often destroyed or highly disrupted, making them effectively indistinguishable
from lithic fragments in CT data.
(ii) Even in cases where an older agglutinate fragment was incorporated in a relatively intact
form, its boundary with the newly formed agglutinitic glass would still be extremely difficult
to identify in CT radiographs. Although previous studies have shown that agglutinitic glasses
from the same sampling site may differ substantially in chemical composition (Basu & McKay,

contrast, the primary physical parameter detected by micro-CT. As a result, older and newly
formed agglutinitic glass typically occupy overlapping grayscale ranges in CT volumes, and
their interface lacks the sharp density discontinuity that characterizes, for example, glass-lithic
boundaries. Consequently, the outlines of older agglutinates cannot be reliably segmented in
our CT data, making it impossible to distinguish them from lithic fragments.
Given these limitations, our fragment content measurements and the subsequent vesicle ratio
calculations inherently treat older incorporated agglutinates as part of the general fragment

emphasize that this limitation is unlikely to affect our conclusions. In our study, we determined

agglutinates. If vesicles preserved within these older agglutinates significantly biased our

(e = 0.11) compared to CE5 (e = 0.23). This inverse relationship indicates that older
CE6 CE5
agglutinates are not the primary factor influencing our vesicle ratio estimates.
We acknowledge this as a limitation of the current study and note that future work combining
micro-CT with targeted EDX or BSE imaging on extracted agglutinates could help better
discriminate older agglutinates, refine interface classifications, and evaluate their influence on

impacts. Laboratory impact experiments show that micrometeorite impacts can generate flash
temperatures of several thousand Kelvin (Eichhorn, 1978). Furthermore, recent silicon isotope
modeling provides quantitative estimates of these transient melt temperatures for lunar regolith:
CE5 soils likely experienced impact-induced temperatures of ~1,200–2,000 K, whereas CE6
and Apollo soils reached even higher temperatures (~2,500–5,000 K) (Zhang et al., 2025a).
These temperatures are fully sufficient to melt and partially vaporize regolith, thereby
generating agglutinates.
We have now clarified this distinction in the revised text and explicitly stated that the transient
temperatures discussed in our study refer to those of hypervelocity impacts, not from diurnal
heating.

cited from previous studies, thereby making the comparison with CE6 clearer and more
coherent.
“Previous research has shown that CE5 samples experienced relatively lower temperatures
(1,200–2,000K, ref. 32) induced by micrometeorite impacts compared to Apollo soil samples88,
although such temperatures are already sufficient to melt regolith and generate agglutinates.
For CE6 samples, the discovery of oldhamite89 and silicon isotope modeling suggests that the
glass formation temperatures are likely comparable to those documented in Apollo samples,
including Apollo 17 (2,500–5,000K, ref. 32,88).”
20. At the end of this paragraph the authors mention potential contributions to vesicle
formation in agglutinates. The authors mention melt viscosity and cooling/welding history.
These can be further elaborated on considering that melt compositions tend towards that of
mafic compositions due to low melting temperatures of basaltic components and that the
cooling history of agglutinitic melt is extremely fast (quenched).
Response: Thanks for this very constructive suggestion. We fully agree that vesicle formation
in agglutinates is closely linked to both melt composition and cooling history, and that these
aspects deserve clearer elaboration.
Previous geochemical studies show that CE5 regolith contains substantially higher abundances
of mafic compositions (42.0 wt% pyroxene, 5.7 wt% olivine, and 4.5 wt% ilmenite) compared
with CE6, which contains only 33.3 wt% pyroxene, 0.5 wt% olivine, and 1.6 wt% ilmenite (Li
et al., 2022; Li et al., 2024). Because these phases have relatively low melting temperatures,
agglutinitic melts derived from CE5 soils are expected to be compositionally more mafic. As a
consequence, CE5 agglutinitic melts likely cooled extremely rapidly, which would have limited
the time window for volatile escape. Under such rapid cooling, vesicles that would otherwise
migrate, coalesce, or collapse may instead become trapped within the melt interior. The
combined effects of mafic-rich melt compositions and ultra-fast quenching therefore provide a
plausible explanation for why CE5 agglutinates may have retained a higher internal porosity.
Revision: We appreciate the reviewer highlighting this mechanism, and we have incorporated
this clarification into the revised manuscript in Lines 420-423:
“An alternative explanation for the higher porosity observed in CE5 agglutinates is that CE5
regolith contain a higher proportion of mafic components24,25, leading to lower melting
temperatures and extremely rapid cooling of agglutinitic melts, which may trap more volatile
gas within the agglutinate interiors.”
21. Paragraph 19: Line 414-415: The authors mention that abrasion preferentially removes
the fragments within agglutinates. How would this affect the Ir value if the vesicles are inherent
to melt, not the fragments.
Response: Thanks for the insightful comment. We apologize that the phrasing in the previous
manuscript may have caused confusion regarding how abrasion and fragmentation affects Ir
values.
To clarify, vesicles within agglutinates can be broadly categorized into three groups:
(i) vesicles formed within the glassy matrix
(ii) vesicles located at interfaces between the glassy matrix and incorporated fragments
(iii) vesicles contained within fragments themselves
The third category is volumetrically minor—our Supplementary Figure 6 shows that most
basalt fragments in CE5 and CE6 have void ratios <2%, and previous studies (Goguen et al.,
2024) similarly report very low particle porosity (<0.3%) in Apollo 11 and Apollo 14 soils.
Thus, the vast majority of vesicles in agglutinates belong to categories (i) and (ii).
Abrasion during gardening preferentially removes the solid fragments embedded within
agglutinates. This process exposes or truncates vesicles located at fragment-glass interfaces,
effectively converting many of these irregular vesicles into open cavities that are no longer
counted toward the internal vesicle statistics used to calculate Ir. As a result, the surviving
vesicles in bulk soil agglutinates are dominated by those formed within the glassy matrix,
which tend to be more regular in morphology (as detailed in our response to Comment #9).
This mechanism likely explains why bulk soil agglutinates exhibit higher Ir values than their
larger counterparts.
Revision: Revised Lines 440-443:
“At the bulk soil scale, this process reduces the abundance of internal fragments, exposes or
removes irregular vesicles, and leaves behind agglutinates dominated by regular vesicles
formed within the glassy matrix, thereby producing higher Ir values (Fig. 3a).”
22. Do CE6 agglutinates generally contain more fragments? Why might this be the case?
Response: Both are good questions. We apologize that our previous phrasing may have
inadvertently created the impression that CE6 agglutinates generally contain more fragments.
This is not the case.
To clarify, we distinguish two categories of agglutinates in our study:
 Larger (selected) agglutinates (>200 μm)
 Bulk soil agglutinates (<200 μm)
For larger agglutinates, the distributions of Ir values for CE5 and CE6 (Response Fig. 4a,
upper panel shown below) show nearly identical means, indicating no systematic difference in
fragment volumetric abundance between CE5 and CE6 for this size class.
For the bulk soil agglutinates, however, Response Figure 4b shows that CE6 exhibits a
distribution shifted toward smaller Ir. Because Ir inversely correlates with fragment abundance,
this pattern suggests that CE6 bulk soil agglutinates may contain more fragments on average.
We recognize that the original legend in Supplementary Fig. 7 (“CE5 agglutinates” vs. “CE6
agglutinates”) was overly general and may have contributed to this misunderstanding. We have
corrected this to specify “bulk soil agglutinates.”
Regarding the possible cause of this difference, we propose the following mechanism: for CE5,
larger agglutinates contain higher internal porosity and larger vesicles (as detailed in our
response to Comment #20). Their fragments are connected by relatively limited amounts of
glassy matrix. Under long-term gardening, shear stresses can induce breakage and preferential
removal of fragment-rich regions, leaving behind more glass-dominated structures with higher
Ir values. For CE6, larger agglutinates contain more densely packed fragments embedded in a
continuous glass matrix. Abrasion dominates their modification, allowing internal fragment
structures to be better preserved. As a result, CE6 bulk soil agglutinates retain slightly more
fragments, consistent with their lower Ir values.
Importantly, we emphasize that this interpretation is inferred from Ir-based observations. While
this explanation is plausible, it is not the only possible scenario. Future work with larger
datasets is required to better quantify the relationship between Ir and Fr, as well as to test this
proposed mechanism more rigorously.
Response Figure 4. a Void ratios and internal regular vesicles fraction (Ir) of selected larger
agglutinates from CE5 (red) and CE6 (blue) lunar samples. The average Ir values of the two
groups are nearly identical, as indicated by vertical solid lines in the upper kernel density plot.
Pentagons indicate average Ir and void ratios of numerous bulk soil agglutinates for CE5 (red;
235 particles) and CE6 (blue; 555 particles), where the higher Ir values observed in CE5
agglutinates may be attributed to differences in internal structure. b Ir distribution of CE5 and
CE6 bulk soil agglutinates.
Revision: Revised Lines 443-447:
“In contrast, CE6 larger agglutinates contain more densely packed fragments embedded in a
continuous glass matrix, and their evolution is governed primarily by abrasion (Supplementary
Fig. 8e, f). These more strongly welded structures are more resistant to fragment loss, which
may help preserve internal fragments in bulk soil agglutinates and result in slightly lower Ir
values compared with CE5 bulk soil agglutinates.”
We have also updated Supplementary Figure 7 to explicitly indicate that the statistics
represent bulk soil agglutinates.
23. Paragraph 20: Line 437-438: Generally, when correlating surface exposure proxies, be
specific as to which ones. In this context, what exactly was grain size fraction compared to.
Response: Good point and thanks for requesting this. After revisiting the relevant literature
(McKay et al., 1974), we confirm that the correlation we referred to concerns the relationship
between mean grain size (<1 cm) and the Is/FeO maturity index, which serves as the specific
surface exposure proxy in this context. We appreciate the reviewer’s suggestion, as our original
phrasing did not make this sufficiently explicit.
Revision: We have revised Lines 465-467 to clearly specify the surface exposure proxy used
in the comparison:
“For impact fragmentation, previous studies have shown a correlation between the Is/FeO value,
a surface exposure proxy, and mean particle size in regolith samples with particle sizes <1 cm
(ref. 72).”
24. Paragraph 21: Line 452-454: I would specify that this saturation affects the bulk size
fraction, as opposed to the entirety of the regolith (i.e. all size fractions).
Response: Thanks for requesting this helpful clarification. You are absolutely right that our
current dataset does not allow us to demonstrate that morphological saturation applies to all
size fractions of the regolith. Our conclusions are constrained to the bulk soil fraction (20–200
µm), which is the size range directly analyzed in this study. We appreciate the reviewer’s
suggestion and have revised the text accordingly to avoid overgeneralization.
Revision: We have updated Lines 480-482 to explicitly limit the inference to the bulk soil
fraction:
“Moreover, the data imply that space weathering-induced morphological modification may
have reached a saturation state within the bulk soil fraction of the youngest and least weathered
CE5 regolith46, with the onset of saturation thus occurring before ~2.2 Ma.”
25. 73002 was found to be largely composed of highlands material with small amounts of
basaltic material found throughout, mostly concentrated near the top 3 cm (Neuman et al., 2025:
Revealing the Moon's Taurus‐Littrow Landslide via Integrated Analysis of Pristine Apollo 17
Soil Core 73001/2). I would clarify that 73002 is compositionally distinct from pure mare
regolith and elaborate on this when making comparisons to Chang'e samples.
Response: Important and constructive comment. Indeed, Apollo 73002 is compositionally
distinct from pure mare regolith, as it contains a substantial proportion of highlands-derived
material with basaltic components concentrated mainly in the uppermost few centimeters, as
pointed out by the reviewer with the timely reference (Neuman et al., 2025). This distinction
is essential when comparing 73002 with the Chang’e-5 and Chang’e-6 mare soils.
We have now explicitly incorporated this clarification into the revised manuscript. At the same
time, we emphasize that despite these compositional differences, our morphometric results
show that large basalt particles (500–700 µm) from 73002 exhibit strong morphological
similarity to those from CE5 and CE6. This agreement provides further support for our
inference that the saturation state may persist even for larger particles in more strongly space-
weathered soils, and even in regolith such as 73002 that includes more complex lithologic
mixtures.
Revision: As suggested, we have elaborated on these points (Lines 482–486):
“To further test this potentially compelling hypothesis, we examined Apollo 17 sample 73002,
collected from the upper ~20 cm of the Light Mantle landslide deposit at the base of the South
Massif in the Taurus–Littrow Valley, a site at the mare-highland boundary characterized by a
substantial proportion of highlands material and basalts of multiple ages90,100.”
As well as in revised Lines 492–495:
“Morphometric results show that the saturation state may persist even for larger particles in
more strongly space-weathered soils, and even in 73002 regolith that is not pure mare material
but instead contains more complex lithologic mixtures (Supplementary Fig. 9).”
26. In Morris et al., 2022, they found that the in situ reworking zone of 73002 had an upper
development age of ~17 Ma. The 3.0 Ma age found in SEP track densities was the average of
exposure ages from individual particles in the core, and not reflective of the overall time
regolith had been subject to regolith gardening. Therefore, it would be more appropriate to
compare the maximum exposure ages of a soil to evaluate the saturation timescales of bulk soil
morphology.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this valuable clarification. We fully agree that
maximum exposure age, rather than average exposure age, provides a more appropriate basis
for evaluating the saturation timescales of bulk soil morphology.
Regarding the ~17 Ma upper development age reported in McFadden et al. (2024), we carefully
traced its derivation. Morris (1978) established a relationship between the depth of the in-situ
reworking zone and its development timescale using combined Is/FeO and 26Al profiles from
Apollo cores:
Dr 2.2

t
0.45
where Dr represents the depth of the in-situ reworking zone (in cm), and t denotes the timescale
for its development. Based on an estimated reworking depth of ~8 cm reported by McFadden
et al. (2024), the corresponding in-situ reworking zone development timescale is calculated to
be ~17 Ma.
However, this value is not equivalent to the maximum exposure age. As we discussed in our
response to Comment #16, the maximum exposure age of ~7.0 Ma (McFadden et al., 2024) is
more directly tied to the 73002 uppermost regolith that experiences the particle reshaping
processes relevant to morphological saturation.
However, the depth of the in-situ reworking zone for 73002 remains somewhat
uncertain, e.g., ~8 cm in McFadden et al. (2024) vs. ~9.5 cm in Morris et al. (2022). Meanwhile,
exposure age measurement is a more mature and widely accepted method for quantifying the
cumulative effect of regolith gardening. For these reasons, we choose maximum exposure age
for evaluating morphological saturation timescales in this study.
We again appreciate the reviewer’s attention to detail and commitment to constructive
feedback, which we hope has greatly improved the clarity and rigor of our study!
Revision: As noted in the Revision to Comment #16, in the revised manuscript we have
replaced all previous mentions of average exposure ages with the corresponding maximum
exposure ages for CE5, CE6, and Apollo 17 (73002).

review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

The lunar mare regolith preserves tripartite records of volcanism, impacting, and space weathering. However, previous studies based on limited soil particle numbers were hindered by issues of sample representativeness. Here we conduct micro-CT scans of bulk soil samples from Chang’e-5 (nearside) and Chang’e-6 (farside), and develop machine learning-based image segmentation and classification methods to identify a vast number of basalt, agglutinate, breccia, and monomineralic particles. The Chang’e-5 basalt exhibits higher plagioclase content than Chang’e-6, while agglutinates from Chang’e-6 have lower void ratios, respectively indicating different lava origins and more intense micrometeorite bombardment for farside Chang’e-6. Despite their contrasting volcanic and impacting histories, the soil particles for these youngest nearside/farside samples exhibit similar morphometric distributions, suggesting that space weathering reached saturation in shaping surficial soil particle morphology in ~2.2 million years or less. These findings may extend to other mare regions and help establish space weathering models for other airless bodies.

---

## Introduction

The lunar mare regolith has been progressively shaped by continuous space weathering since the Moon’s formation1,2. From the sampling efforts of the Apollo, Luna, and Chang’e missions, it is now well established that the mare regolith comprises primarily basalt, meteorite impact melt breccia, micrometeorite impact agglutinates, and monomineralic fragments3–5. The mineralogical and chemical compositions of mare basalts are directly linked to the nature of initial igneous magmatic processes—mantle source melting, the extent of magmatic fractional crystallization in the magma chamber, and degassing during volcanic eruption6–10—while their internal vesicle structures provide clues to volcanic eruption dynamics and the relative distance from source vents11. Following flow emplacement, the mare surface has undergone prolonged modification by meteorite impacts and solar wind irradiation12–14. During impacting, the lunar regolith is imparted with cumulative kinetic energy, which progressively fragments and abrades the lunar bedrock, a process referred to here as “comminution”15. Accompanying impacts, molten glass produced by micrometeorite collisions aggregates finer regolith particles, forming agglutinates16. Agglutinates are irregularly shaped and contain vesicles that not only modulate volatile escape and encode the thermomechanical conditions of micrometeorite bombardment17, but also serve as nanoscale reservoirs capable of storing and mobilizing solar wind-derived hydrogen and water18.

Meanwhile, fragmentation and abrasion continuously reshape particle morphologies19,20, encoding the cumulative effects of space weathering on airless bodies21. On the Moon, the fraction of lunar regolith with particle sizes <1 mm is particularly relevant to surface space weathering22 and warrants detailed investigation. Due to limitations in current analytical techniques as encountered in this study, it remains challenging to obtain reliable morphometric data for particle sizes <20 μm (ref. 23), which are typically classified as “lunar dust”(see Methods). Particles within the 20–20 μm size range, comprising over 60% of the <1 mm fraction, are defined as the “bulk soil” fraction24,25, while the remaining particles (>200 μm) are categorized as “large particles”. Notably, this dominance of the bulk soil fraction is also observed in Apollo samples and can be attributed to the progressive consumption of the lunar dust fraction during agglutinate formation and its subsequent redistribution within the bulk soil fraction22. As such, the bulk soil fraction serves as the primary reservoir of surface evolution signatures on the Moon. The morphology of particles within this fraction not only preserves tripartite records of volcanism, impacting, and space weathering, but also exerts a critical influence on its geomechanical behavior26. Moreover, accurate morphological data serve as a key input for building high-fidelity predictive simulations of the Moon’s surface, enabling predictive simulations of regolith behavior under various exploration scenarios27.

On December 1, 2020, China’s Chang’e-5 (CE5) mission28 landed at 43.06°N, 51.92°W in northern Oceanus Procellarum and returned 1,731 g of regolith (Fig. 1a-b). On June 25, 2024, the Chang’e-6 (CE6) mission24 collected 1,935.3 g of sample materials from the South Pole–Aitken basin (41.625°S, 153.978°W) via both scooping and drilling (Fig. 1a, c). These two missions provided the first paired youngest mare regolith samples (<3 Ga) from the lunar near and far sides29,30, allowing a rare opportunity to construct a unified model of regolith evolution under comparable analytical conditions. Geochronology, geochemistry, and remote sensing data suggest that the CE5 regolith is locally derived and basaltic, with intermediate-Ti basalts10,25, whereas CE6 soils contain a greater proportion of exotic components, including not only local basalts, mainly low- to intermediate-Ti basalts but also noritic and other components24,31. Silicon isotopes further reveal that the CE6 site may have undergone more intense micrometeorite bombardment than the CE5 region32.

Despite extensive study, debate continues over the classification of basalt and the evolution of space weathering in CE5 and CE6 regolith particles. At the heart of these issues are two challenges presented by previous methods: (i) the representativeness of traditional thin-section-based geochemical analyses, which yield only two-dimensional particle data and rely on hand-picked grains; and (ii) the applicability of mineral-scale analyses and interpretations to the evolution of the whole lunar regolith in the region. In recent years, the growing accessibility of micro-computed tomography (micro-CT) has enabled its widespread application in lunar soil research33–37. As a non-destructive technique, micro-CT scanning allows for high-resolution reconstruction of both external particle 3D morphology and internal structures of each individual particle within the bulk soil. It enables precise quantification of the 3D morphometrics of numerous individual particles23,38–40. Recently, machine learning approaches also have also been introduced to segment large numbers of lunar regolith particles from micro-CT radiographs23,39.

It is widely accepted that space weathering exerts a strong influence on the morphology of rock fragments on airless bodies41–43. However, this paradigm may not be directly applicable to the lunar surface, where particle morphology is simultaneously governed by the primary lava composition, impacting history, and the cumulative intensity of space weathering. Variations in primary lava composition give rise to distinct mineralogical assemblages in lunar regolith, which in turn affect particle-scale mechanical responses to space weathering. For instance, plagioclase is more susceptible to brittle fracture than pyroxene, rendering plagioclase-rich basalts and breccias more prone to crack formation and localized abrasion, thereby influencing particle morphology during meteoroid bombardment15,44. At the microscale, different mineral phases also exhibit varying responses to space weathering processes such as solar wind implantation, localized melting, and vaporization45,46, further modifying particle morphology47,48. Additionally, differences in impact energy across the lunar surface produce varying degrees of lithologic fragmentation and regolith gardening effects, both of which significantly affect particle morphology49. Importantly, the mineralogical composition of local regolith is a key factor influencing agglutinate abundance. During rapid, non-equilibrium impact melting, low-melting-temperature mafic minerals such as ilmenite, pyroxene, and olivine are more readily incorporated into impact melts than high-melting-temperature plagioclase50,51. As a result, soils with higher plagioclase contents may produce fewer agglutinates50. The regolith maturity also exerts a strong control on agglutinate abundance, with more mature soils typically containing higher proportions of agglutinates22. Together, these factors influence agglutinate abundance and, consequently, the overall particle-scale morphological characteristics of regolith. Thus, the morphology of lunar regolith particles represents an integrated signature of sampling site geological and space weathering processes. Critically, the lack of comprehensive morphological data across different sampling sites has hindered the ability to disentangle these factors. To rigorously assess the morphological consequences of space weathering, assessing a vast number of particles is required, and comparative study of particle morphology across different lunar regions is urgently needed.

In this study, we apply micro-CT scans to bulk soil from the CE5 (CE5C0400YJFM01001) and CE6 (CE6C0200YJFM008) samples under identical settings, and use machine learning approaches to segment and classify individual particles in the scans. This standardized, non-destructive workflow enables high-precision quantification of 3D morphometrics and internal structures across multiple particle types. Several intrinsic limitations of micro-CT data processing are addressed in our study design. First, segmentation accuracy must be maintained across a wide range of particle sizes to ensure the fidelity of measured morphometrics. Second, the classification algorithm must operate on accurately segmented particles while retaining their internal textures, thereby enabling refined categorization and more refined interpretations of regolith formation and space weathering processes. These challenges are explicitly accounted for in our analysis. Based on this comprehensive dataset, we develop a model for the formation and evolutionary processes of the surficial mare regolith, revealing that space weathering drives morphology saturation at the particle scale across diverse particle types. Our findings provide important insights into the temporal trajectory of lunar surface modification and the convergent morphological pathways induced by prolonged space weathering.

## Results

Mineralogical differences between CE5 and CE6 basalts
Based on returned mare soils24,30 and lunar orbiter data52, basalts represent the dominant particle type within lunar mare soils and can also be used to reconstruct the thermochemical volcanic history of the Moon7,53. Among basaltic textures, subophitic and poikilitic types (Fig. 2a, b) are readily distinguished due to their relatively large crystal sizes and dominate the basaltic population, and can also be accurately classified using machine learning algorithms23–25,40. Basalt fragments, which are also prevalent (Fig. 2b), exhibit distinct striped textures that facilitate their recognition. Mineral phase densities in basalts can also be effectively distinguished through CT radiographs (Fig. 2b, c), enabling clear separation into high-density (Hp), medium-density (Mp), and low-density (Lp) phases based on grayscale intensity. Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) analyses further confirm that the Hp correspond to ilmenite, the Mp to olivine or pyroxene, and the Lp to plagioclase (Supplementary Fig. 2f, n and o). These three phases constitute the principal mineralogical components of lunar mare basalts30,54.

Based on analyses of 5,605 basalt particles from bulk soils (considering only intact particles, with edge-truncated particles excluded; Supplementary Video 1; Supplementary Video 2), the volume fractions of Hp, Mp, and Lp in CE5 basalts were determined as 6.80%, 53.84%, and 39.36%, respectively, and 7.16%, 61.52%, and 31.32% for CE6 (Fig. 2d). As shown in the ternary plot, the 95% probability density contour encompass all discrete basalt data points previously reported from single-particle geochemical analyses of the CE5 and CE6 samples25,30,54. The large dataset provided here offers an effective supplement to the more limited, discrete basaltic data derived from traditional geochemical methods applied to Apollo and Chang’e series soils. As products of continuous meteoritic impacting of a likely diverse range of cooled lava flows, basalt particles in bulk soils collectively preserve the original mineralogical signatures of lavas, enabling reliable classification of local basalt types. Notably, significant mineralogical differences are observed between CE5 and CE6 basalts, with the latter containing a lower abundance of plagioclase, which contributes to its higher density (Supplementary Fig. 4). Previous studies have suggested that both the CE5 and CE6 lavas experienced high degrees of fractional crystallization10,31. But the observed differences in plagioclase content may reflect varying degrees of this process between the two regions.

Traditionally, mare basalts have been classified based on major-element abundances. Electron probe microanalysis data indicate that TiO2 and Al2O3 are primarily hosted in ilmenite (Hp) and plagioclase (Lp), respectively30,54. For large basalt particles suitable for geochemical analysis and hand-picking, linear relationships exist between ilmenite volume fraction and bulk TiO2 content, and between plagioclase volume fraction and bulk Al2O3 content (Supplementary Fig. 5d, e). Applying these linear relationships, we determined bulk TiO2 and Al2O3 contents of 6.08 wt% and 11.60 wt% for CE5 basalts, and 6.17 wt% and 9.43 wt% for CE6, respectively (Fig. 2e). Compared to CE6 lunar soil, CE5 exhibits considerably elevated Al concentrations, consistent with previous findings31, thus likely categorizing CE5 mare basalts as medium-Ti and high-Al types, whereas CE6 basalts correspond to the medium-Ti and low-Al basalts, based on mare basalt classification criteria55. Both samples are assigned to Eratosthenian-aged mare basalts, whose TiO2 abundances are higher than those of typical low- to medium-Ti Apollo basalts, yet lower than those of high-Ti Apollo basalts (Fig. 2e). This distinction supports the interpretation that late-stage lunar volcanism (<3 Ga) involved distinct lava sources and evolutionary pathways from those recorded by Apollo basalts56. Analysis of the internal pore structures of basalts with equivalent diameters >50 μm reveal that the vast majority of void ratios in both CE5 and CE6 basalts are <2% (Supplementary Fig. 6). Such exceptionally low porosity values are characteristic of solidified, non-vesicular coherent mare basalts11, likely formed as a result of CE5 and CE6 lavas having erupted and been emplaced at considerable distances from the source vents as flat, smooth-surfaced flows with low vesicularity, which subsequently cooled into dense basaltic units11.

Distinct internal vesicles of agglutinates in CE5 and CE6 soils
Agglutinates are special regolith particles consisting of smaller lunar soil fragments (mineral particles, rock clasts, and older agglutinates) bonded together by vesicular, flow-banded glass57. They form primarily through micrometeorite-induced melting, which generates vesiculated agglutinitic glass matrices. The vesicles within these matrices are widely interpreted as the combined textural products of solar wind implantation, which generates small vesicles along particle margins, and volatile gas exsolution during melt generation and quenching, which produces larger internal vesicles17,57. Within glassy matrices, sub-microscopic metallic iron nanoparticles (npFe) form through a combination of micrometeorite impact58, solar wind (induced sputtering and reduction)59, transient thermal-spike (driven reduction)60, and externally triggered Fe2+ disproportionation61, all of which collectively modify the optical and magnetic properties of the soil. As such, agglutinates preserve detailed records of space weathering. Agglutinates occur across a wider range of particle sizes within bulk soils. Larger agglutinates (equivalent diameter >200 μm) can be easily isolated manually, whereas smaller agglutinates in bulk soil (equivalent diameter <200 μm) are typically irregular, fragile, and thus challenging to manually extract and analyze. However, this difficulty is overcome with CT scanning, as the distinctive morphological features and abundant internal porosity of agglutinates are readily identifiable in radiographs.

To further investigate agglutinate internal structure, we performed high-resolution micro-CT scans on 84 manually selected larger agglutinates (42 from CE5 and 42 from CE6). Additionally, 3D models were also acquired of numerous bulk soil agglutinates (236 from CE5 and 555 from CE6). Within the glassy regions, vesicles predominantly exhibit regular geometries (EI < 1.7, FI < 1.7, S > 0.9), whereas at the interfaces between glassy matrix and embedded fragments, vesicles become highly irregular (EI > 1.7, FI > 1.7, S < 0.9) (Fig. 3e; calculation methods for EI, FI, and S morphometrics are detailed in Methods, with illustrative examples shown in Supplementary Fig. 10). This contrast likely arises because vesicles forming within relatively homogeneous glassy regions tend to adopt regular shapes controlled by surface tension, whereas vesicles near fragment-glass interfaces are mechanically constrained by surrounding fragments and thus develop irregular morphologies. This phenomenon is also evident in SE imaging of Apollo 11 agglutinates62. To quantify this distinction, we define the internal regular void fraction (Ir) as the proportion of regular vesicles relative to the total vesicle count of a single agglutinate. As agglutinates are composed of both fragments and a glassy matrix63, the glassy matrix and fragment contents (Fr) are inherently volumetrically complementary. This parameter thus may also relate to the volumetric abundance of internal fragments. To assess this possibility, we manually annotated fragments within selected larger agglutinates (Supplementary Fig. 8a, d), finding a strong inverse correlation between Ir and Fr (Fig. 3b). Based on Ir values, we categorize agglutinates into three classes: (i) those with Ir < 0.35 are fragmentation-defined as high fragment content agglutinates (Fig. 3c), (ii) those with Ir > 0.5 are vitrifaction-defined as low fragment content agglutinates (Fig. 3f), and (iii) those with intermediate Ir values (0.35–0.5) are classified as medium fragment-content agglutinates (Fig. 3d). For the broader population of bulk soil agglutinates, Ir was directly used as a proxy to estimate internal fragment abundance.

Our results show no significant differences in the distribution or mean Ir values between the larger agglutinates of CE5 and CE6, where Ir ≈ Ir = 0.42 (Fig. 3a). However, internal porosity measurements consistently show a considerable lower average void ratio in CE6 agglutinates (e = 0.11) compared to those from CE5 (e = 0.23) (Fig. 3a). For agglutinates in bulk soils, Ir values are higher in CE5 (Ir = 0.49) than in CE6 (Ir = 0.46). Compared to their larger counterparts, the bulk soil agglutinates from CE5 exhibit a modest increase in Ir values, suggesting a relatively lower internal fragment content (Fig. 3a). Given that bulk soil agglutinates likely represent the fragmented products of larger agglutinates64, this trend may reflect inherent structural differences in the initial agglutinates of the two regions, which could in turn influence their subsequent response to space weathering.

Morphological homogenization among similar lunar regolith particle types
The morphology of lunar regolith particles records long-term space weathering processes on the lunar surface23. Using machine learning segmentation and classification methods, we obtain morphometrics—aspect ratio, sphericity, convexity, and roundness—with definitions provided in the Methods and Supplementary Fig. 10, for no fewer than 100 individual effective and intact particles from each particle category from both CE5 and CE6 bulk soil CT scans, ensuring statistically representative datasets for each particle type. The analyzed particle types include basalts, agglutinates, breccias, high-density (Hm), medium-density (Mm), and low-density (Lm) monomineralic particles, as well as glass beads (Fig. 4a). The Hm, Mm, and Lm groups are readily distinguishable in radiographs based on their X-ray attenuation intensities, where Hm is primarily composed of the opaque Fe-oxide mineral ilmenite, Mm mainly represented by pyroxene, olivine, or anisotropic glass, and Lm consists predominantly of plagioclase grains23,65. Breccias were also included; however, due to their limited abundance, their morphometric distributions may not be statistically robust. Glass beads were omitted, given their highly regular, nearly spherical shapes, with morphometrics closely approximating those of ideal spheres (Fig. 4a). To examine potential size-dependent effects, Mm and Lm particles were subdivided into larger (equivalent diameter > 50 μm) and smaller (equivalent diameter < 50 μm) fractions. Our results show that aspect ratio is virtually unaffected by particle size, while sphericity and convexity exhibit only minor size dependence. In contrast, roundness is strongly influenced by particle size, with smaller particles being rounder (Fig. 4c). This trend likely reflects the scale-dependent nature of morphological descriptors and is consistent with observations from Apollo lunar soil studies37.

Our morphology results also indicate remarkable consistency across the distributions of all morphometrics for basalt, breccia, agglutinate, Hm, Mm (both size fractions), and Lm (both size fractions) particles from CE5 and CE6 soils (Fig. 4b, c). Differences in mean morphometrics for corresponding particle categories between the two sites are all within 5% (Supplementary Table 3). The overall regularity (OR) of different particle types exhibits two distinct regimes. More than half of the basalt and monomineralic particles (Hm, Mm, and Lm), in terms of particle number, fall within an OR range of 0.63–0.75 (Fig. 4d). These particle types represent the majority of the bulk soil population (>60 vol%). These particles, characterized by simple internal structure, are herein referred to as “simple particles.” In contrast, breccia and agglutinates display considerably lower OR values than other particle types, indicating a markedly more irregular morphology (Fig. 4d). Owing to their complex internal structure, these particles are categorized as “complex particles.” Using the same methods applied to the lunar regolith, we additionally analyzed the morphometric distributions of a large number of particles from the lunar regolith simulant (LRS: IGG-01), which was produced by mechanically crushing basalt66. Compared to lunar basalt particles, the LRS particles exhibit lower aspect ratios (Fig. 4b). Such characteristics are consistent with the angular-to-subrounded morphologies observed on asteroid regolith surfaces, where particles typically experience short surface residence times and limited abrasion67,68. This similarity likely reflects the fact that both mechanically crushed simulants and asteroid regolith are dominated by relatively “fresh” fragments that have not undergone prolonged regolith gardening.

Building on particle classification, we quantified the relative abundances of each particle type (Fig. 4e). In particular, agglutinate abundance can serve as an indicator of soil maturity57. This parameter correlates positively with the maturity index Is/FeO, but only when Is/FeO < 60, above which agglutinate abundance is known to saturate in highly mature soils69,70. The CE5 bulk soil exhibits an Is/FeO value of ~14, consistent with immature soils71, and an agglutinate abundance of ~8%. In contrast, CE6 soils yield an Is/FeO value of ~56.5, characteristic of mature soils72, together with a higher agglutinate abundance of ~17%. The elevated agglutinate abundance and Is/FeO value of CE6 are consistent with trends established in previous studies70. Furthermore, the Is/FeO index is closely linked to the abundance of npFe, produced on grain rims and within agglutinates by micrometeorite bombardment and solar wind sputtering/redeposition, and therefore reflects the cumulative intensity of these space weathering processes. Another critical component of space weathering is regolith “gardening” driven by meteorite impacts, which is commonly expressed through the surface soil maximum exposure age, where soils with longer exposure durations experience more extensive overturn and reworking73. According to regolith evolution models, CE5 surface soils have a maximum exposure age of ~2.2 Ma, whereas CE6 soils have been exposed since ~3.2 Ma (ref. 74). The slightly longer exposure duration of CE6 regolith suggests a greater degree of surface soil gardening, and together with these maturity indices, consistently demonstrates that CE6 soils have experienced a higher overall degree of space weathering.
