Response: Thanks for highlighting this important issue. We acknowledge that in the original
version we did not provide a sufficiently clear rationale for subdividing lunar regolith into
“lunar dust,” “bulk soil,” and “large particles.”
The definition of “lunar dust” follows the commonly adopted convention of particles
smaller than 20 μm (Sun et al., 2017; Wallace et al., 2009). Although this fraction is an essential
component of the regolith, the extremely small size makes it difficult to capture morphological
information at scale with current micro-CT techniques. In this study, therefore, we treat this
group primarily as the end-product of space weathering.
For the “large particles” fraction, we defined the lower threshold at 200 μm based on the
relatively low abundance of such particles in the CE5 and CE6 soils. As shown in Reply Figure
3, particles larger than 200 μm account for <15% of the total regolith volume. Within the bulk
soil micro-CT framework adopted here, this fraction yields only a limited number of
measurable particles, which constrains the statistical robustness of their morphometric
distributions. Nonetheless, this does not imply that large particles are excluded from the
saturation in morphological modification of space weathering, as we have further elaborated in
our response to Comment 1(2).
By contrast, the 20–200 μm fraction constitutes the dominant component of the CE5 and
CE6 soils, accounting for >60% of the total regolith volume. This size range therefore
represents the principal carrier of surface-evolutionary signatures and provides the most
statistically robust basis for morphometric analysis. Accordingly, we refer to this interval as
the “bulk soil fraction” and focus on it as the primary foundation for our model.

subdivided into large particles (equivalent diameter >200 μm), bulk soil (20–200 μm), and

(4) Lastly, the authors suggest that morphological saturation has occurred by ~2 Ga, but this
claim lacks direct comparison with older Apollo regolith particles. Without examining whether
Apollo particles also exhibit similar morphometrics, it is difficult to confidently conclude that
the saturation has been reached. Why don’t the authors interpret the observed morphological
similarity between CE5 and CE6 simply due to their similar ages?
Response: Thanks for raising this constructive and important point. We fully acknowledge that
this was a limitation of the previous version of our manuscript, as we were unable to directly
access Apollo soils for micro-CT scanning test under the same experimental conditions, and
therefore could not provide solid first-hand evidence for morphological saturation. However,
additionally inspired by Reviewer #2’s Comment 29, we realized that the formation age of the
Chang’e basalts (CE5 ~2.0 Ga, CE6 ~2.8 Ga) is not directly linked to the extent of space
weathering experienced by the regolith. For example, if an impact event occurred in the mare
undergone 100 million years of space weathering, irrespective of the basalt crystallization age
10
(Morris, 1978). Consequently, in the revised manuscript we describe the degree of space
weathering using a multi-proxy suite of maturity indicators, including agglutinate abundance,
Is/FeO values, and surface exposure ages of the regolith (see revision to Comment 1(1)). The
dominant process influencing particle morphology is impact gardening, and as McFadden et al.
(2024) emphasize, where its effect on the modification of the surface regolith is best captured
by surface exposure ages. We therefore characterize morphological saturation primarily in
terms of surface exposure age.
To address the reviewer’s concern regarding the absence of Apollo soils in our dataset, we
adopted a compromise approach. The Apollo missions returned 382 kg of material from six
sites, comprising ~2,200 individual samples. Although nearly all of these samples have been
examined, a few remained unopened until recently (Eckley et al., 2025). Among these was the
Apollo 17 double drive tube 73001/2, which sampled regolith to ~70 cm depth in the Light
Mantle landslide deposit at the base of the South Massif in Taurus-Littrow Valley. The upper
section (73002) was opened and scanned by micro-CT in 2019, with experimental data
subsequently released (Eckley et al., 2025). Previous work indicates that 73002 sampled
several basalt flows, and its surface maturity is well constrained: the uppermost regolith
exhibits an Is/FeO value of ~74 (Morris et al., 2022) and a surface exposure age of ~3.0 Ma
(McFadden et al., 2024). In comparison, CE5 soils show an Is/FeO value of ~14 and an
exposure age of ~1.5 Ma (Qian et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025b), while CE6 soils exhibit an
Is/FeO of ~56.5 and an exposure age of ~2.1 Ma (Zhang et al., 2025b; Li et al., 2025). Thus,
the Apollo 17 sample is more mature than both CE5 and CE6, and its derivation from a
landslide deposit ensures mineralogical and lithological complexity. If morphological
saturation is still observed in 73002 surface regolith particles, it would imply that such
saturation can be achieved by the relatively short exposure age of CE5 (~1.5 Ma).
It should be noted, however, that the Apollo 73002 CT radiographs were acquired at a
resolution of 25.8 μm (Eckley et al., 2025; Reply Figure 4a). This restricts morphological
characterization to particles larger than ~500 μm, precluding direct comparison with the bulk
soil fraction (20–200 μm) analyzed in this study. To enable meaningful comparison, we
therefore selected basalt particles in the 500–700 μm range from both CE5 and CE6 soils, using
basalt as the target material (see also response to Comment 1(2)).
For CE5 and CE6, which are shallow scoop samples with limited large particle populations,
we manually selected ~200 particles each, yielding 22 basalt grains from CE5 and 27 from
CE6. For 73002, we restricted our analysis to the uppermost ~3 cm of regolith, to both match
the near-surface context of CE5 and CE6 and to ensure strong space weathering effects. Basalt
grains were readily identified in the radiographs (Reply Figure 4b), manually extracted, and
reconstructed in 3D for morphometric analysis (Reply Figure 4c–d). The larger sample size
available from Apollo 73002 allowed us to extract 110 basalt particles, ensuring robust
statistics.
Our morphometric results (Reply Figure 2b–e) reveal highly similar distributions of AR,
S, Cx, and R across Apollo 17 large basalts and those from CE5 and CE6. The mean values
differ by <10%, with comparable standard deviations. This result suggests that morphological
saturation is already established by the CE5 surface exposure age of ~1.5 Ma. Nevertheless,
we emphasize that further validation with larger CE5 and CE6 datasets is required to test this
conclusion in future work.

2. On regolith particle evolution processes:
In paragraph [20], the authors note that impact gardening, thermal cycling, and solar wind
irradiation contribute to fragmentation and abrasion. However, the role of agglomeration
processes is not discussed. For example, breccia particles may be formed by the strong
12
compression due to meteoroid impact, and agglutinate particles are formed by the gathering of
partly melted fragments. Also, fragmentation and abrasion can have opposing effects on
particle morphology. Such processes must be considered to accurately evaluate regolith
evolution. The current interpretation risks oversimplifying the particle evolution process.
Response: Very insightful comment. We fully agree that our initial version of Figure 5 and the
associated discussion in paragraph [20] oversimplified the mechanisms underlying
morphological equilibrium, as we did not adequately address the role of impact agglutination,
nor did we provide sufficient discussion of the contrasting effects of fragmentation and
abrasion. As the reviewer correctly notes, agglutination plays a critical role in the formation of
breccias and agglutinates, while fragmentation and abrasion may exert opposing influences on
particle morphology. The omission of these aspects in our initial submission indeed made our
conceptual model less comprehensive.
In the revised manuscript, we have restructured our discussion of morphological saturation
mechanisms to provide a more complete representation of lunar surface processes. Specifically,
particle reshaping mechanisms now include the following.
 Impact gardening (mainly abrasion caused by repeated interactions among numerous
grains within the regolith)
 Impact fragmentation (grain breakage via direct energy deposition during impacts)
 Impact agglutination (fusion of surrounding grains into breccias or agglutinates due to
impact-induced melts or semi-plastic phases)
 Impact sputtering (deposits from impact events appearing randomly on the surface of
minerals, forming a sputtering deposit layer that modifies particle morphology)
 Impact abrasion (localized surface wear caused by micrometeoroid strikes or secondary
impacts that generate linear scratches)
 Thermal fatigue (fracturing and disintegration from diurnal thermal stresses)
 Solar wind irradiation (implantation of high-energy ions producing lattice defects, which
increase susceptibility to subsequent weathering-induced reshaping; in addition, sputtering
by the solar wind which may also erode particle surfaces)
Among these processes, impact agglutination is particularly distinctive as it transforms
“simple particles” into “complex particles” in a cumulative manner, producing irregular
aggregates that strongly affect overall regolith morphology. Other processes generally reshape
particles without altering their fundamental type, although “complex particles” may shed small
fragments that revert to “simple particles”. Both particle types are subsequently subject to
further modification by the full suite of processes.
Regarding the relative influence of fragmentation and abrasion, previous studies
demonstrate that surface exposure age correlates with the grain size of lunar regolith in the >1
mm fraction (Morris et al., 1976; McKay et al., 1974), but this relationship weakens below the
centimetre scale. Furthermore, Weibull statistics show that smaller grains require
disproportionately higher stresses to fail completely (Weibull, 1951; McDowell et al., 2000).
This result implies that for lunar regolith dominated by <1 mm particles, impact fragmentation
is limited, and the majority of impact energy is redistributed into broad-scale impact gardening,
which thus emerges as the primary driver of morphological modification.
Despite marked differences in age, geological setting, basaltic source regions,
micrometeorite flux, and solar wind exposure between CE5 and CE6 sites, the morphometrics
of corresponding particle types remain remarkably consistent. This convergence strongly
suggests that long-term particle reshaping, governed primarily by impact gardening with
contributions from agglutination, drives both “simple” and “complex” particles toward stable
morphologies, such that additional space weathering exerts only minor influence on particle
morphometrics (Reply Figure 5).

4. On the Interpretation of Agglutinate Porosity Differences:
The discussion in paragraphs [18] and [19] are largely speculative. Paragraph [18] explains the
lower internal porosity observed in CE6 agglutinates from the different micrometeorite
bombardment condition in nearside and farside. This can be proved by comparing with the data

contents, and gas escape efficiency is mentioned, but the argument lacks cohesion and empirical support. These sections would benefit from a clearer presentation and more cautious language regarding the proposed mechanisms.
Response: Thanks for this insightful comment. In paragraph [18], we noted that previous
research has shown CE5 soils experienced relatively lower temperatures as induced by
micrometeorite impacts compared to Apollo soils (Nie et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2022). In
contrast, silicon isotope modeling suggests that for CE6 soils, the impact-induced glass
formation temperatures—primarily controlled by micrometeorite impact velocities—are likely
comparable to those documented for Apollo soils (Zhang et al., 2025a). We hypothesized that
the higher glass formation temperatures associated with more intense micrometeorite
bombardment at the CE6 landing site may have contributed to the lower agglutinate void ratios
observed in CE6 relative to CE5.
The reviewer’s suggestion to verify this hypothesis using Apollo data is particularly
valuable. Since our CE5–CE6 comparison already uses Apollo soils as a benchmark, Apollo
samples provide an excellent reference dataset for agglutinate porosity. We selected an Apollo
17 sample (73002) for this comparison because this site is incorporated in the thermal modeling
of Nie et al. (2024). Following the same analytical procedures described in response to
Fig. 6a–b) and calculated their void ratios using the same methodology as for CE5 and CE6.

Finally, regarding paragraphs [18–19], we agree with the reviewer that the original
discussion linking agglutinate structure, volatile contents, and gas escape efficiency lacked
coherence and empirical support. We have substantially revised this section to present a
mechanism-based, but non-exclusive, interpretation.
In silicate melts, lower viscosity—typically at higher temperatures—facilitates bubble
ascent, coalescence, and the development of permeable vesicle networks, allowing for efficient
open-system degassing once pathways connect to the atmospheric vacuum (Harris et al., 2008;
Gonnermann & Manga, 2013). In micrometeorite-formed agglutinates, transient melt films can
enable gases to vent through connected vesicles before cooling; when degassing is efficient,
the resulting internal porosity can be significantly reduced compared to less-degassed clasts
(Rust et al., 2004).
We now interpret the lower porosity of CE6 agglutinates as consistent with (rather than
proving) more efficient syn-formation gas escape under open-system conditions. At the same
time, we explicitly acknowledge alternative explanations, including viscosity contrasts during
18
formation, variations in melt fraction, vesicle connectivity, and post-formation vesicle collapse.
We also clarify that we do not directly measure volatile contents in this study; our inference is
textural and mechanistic, supported by established degassing literature. These clarifications
have been incorporated into the revised manuscript, with appropriately cautious language.

Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for pointing out this important issue. We
acknowledge that in the original version we did not clearly explain the basis for subdividing
lunar regolith into “lunar dust,” “bulk soil,” and “large particles.” The definition of “lunar dust”
follows the commonly adopted convention that classifies particles’ equivalent diameter smaller
than 20 μm (Sun et al., 2017; Wallace et al., 2009). Although this fraction is an essential
component of the regolith, its extremely small size makes large-scale morphological analysis
difficult. In this study, therefore, we treat this group primarily as the end-product of space
weathering.
For the “large particles” fraction, we establish a threshold based on the relatively low
volume percentage of particles’ equivalent diameter >200 μm in the CE5 and CE6 soils. As
shown in Reply Figure 1, such particles account for <15% of the total regolith volume. Within
the bulk soil micro-CT framework adopted in this study, this fraction yields only a limited
number of measurable particles, making robust statistical analysis of their morphology
challenging. Nonetheless, this does not imply that large particles are excluded from the
saturation in morphological modification of space weathering, as we further discuss in response
to Comment #28-29.
By contrast, the 20–200 μm fraction constitutes the dominant component of the CE5 and
CE6 soils, accounting for >60% of the total volume. This size range therefore represents the
main carrier of surface-evolutionary signatures and is the primary focus of our analysis, which
we refer to as the “bulk soil fraction.”

The microstructure of lunar micrometeoroid impact craters (Noble et al. 2016).
Response: Thanks for this valuable recommendation. We have incorporated both references
and briefly summarize their key contributions to grain-scale morphological transformations
under space weathering. Keller & McKay (1997) used TEM to show that most lunar soil
particles develop nanometer-scale surface rims (typically ~60–200 nm) that fall into four end-
member types: amorphous (solar-wind irradiation damage with preferential cation sputtering),
inclusion-rich (impact-vapor–deposited, containing abundant npFe0), multiple (irradiation
layer overlain by vapor-deposited material), and vesicular (abundant <50 nm vesicles from
evolved implanted gases following pulse heating). These rims, and especially npFe0,
systematically modify surface texture and optical/magnetic properties, directly linking
microstructure to macroscopic “maturity” signals.
Noble et al. (2016) characterized natural micrometeoroid microcraters on lunar grains and
documented melt linings (~0.5–2 µm), recrystallized layers, extensive shock-damaged zones
extending up to tens of micrometers, near-surface vesiculation, annealing of solar-flare tracks,
and pervasive npFe0 (~3–7 nm) in melt/recrystallized layers, demonstrating how localized
melting, vapor deposition, and shock collectively reshape grain surfaces and rims at the
nanoscale.

highlight more evidence that suggests these things are related. Maybe don’t include the micro-

answer. Also, it would be good to succinctly state your hypothesis here.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this constructive guidance. In the revised Introduction,
we clarify the connections between mineralogy, space weathering, impact processes, and
resulting particle shape, and we support these links with additional references. Variations in
primary lava composition yield distinct mineralogical assemblages in lunar regolith, which in
turn govern particle-scale mechanical responses to impact processes. For example, plagioclase
is more prone to brittle fracture than pyroxene, rendering plagioclase-rich basalts and breccias
more susceptible to crack propagation and localized abrasion during meteoroid bombardment
(Hörz et al., 1984; Taylor et al., 2001). At the microscale, individual mineral phases respond
differently to space weathering processes such as solar-wind implantation, localized melting,
and vaporization, further altering particle morphology (Denevi et al., 2023; Cao et al., 2025).
In addition, spatial variations in impact energy across the lunar surface drive differences in
lithologic fragmentation and regolith gardening, both of which significantly influence particle
shape (Papike et al., 1982). Taken together, we emphasize that regolith particle morphology
encodes an integrated signature of local geological context and cumulative space weathering
modification.
Following the reviewer’s suggestion, we have relocated the mention of micro-CT (a
methodological tool) to paragraph [6], which focuses on the analytical workflow. To further
maintain a coherent narrative, we also now state our working hypothesis succinctly at the end
of paragraph [6], allowing this paragraph to focus solely on framing the scientific motivation
and evidential basis of the study.

22. Line 158: What is the difference between internal pore structure and a vesicle? How does

Response: We thank the reviewer for raising this important point. In our manuscript, the term
pore structure in basalts refers specifically to internal closed cavities, which is consistent with

agglutinates by replacing “pores” with “vesicles” to avoid confusion, whereas for basalts we

agglutinates, consistent with the usage adopted by Kiefer et al. (2012).
According to Head et al. (2020), mare basalt protolith types include: solidified
nonvesicular coherent mare basalt; inflated flows: surface topography, vesicularity, and
mesoporosity-macroporosity; inflated flows: second boiling, vertical bubble migration and
extrusion of magmatic foam; foam flows and autoregolith formation, foam flows with coherent
surfaces, pyroclastic layers, emplacement of anomalous xenolithic volcanic glass beads, and
volcanic pit crater floor surfaces. Among these, Apollo 12 basalt sample 12038 (Neal et al.,
1994) is a well-documented example of a solidified non-vesicular coherent mare basalt (Head
et al., 2020). XCT analysis of basalts from this sample (Reply Figure 4a) further confirms its
relatively dense interior, with a void ratio of only 3.8% (Gawronska et al., 2022). In comparison,
the CE5 and CE6 basalts analyzed here exhibit even lower porosities (<2%), supporting their
classification as solidified non-vesicular coherent mare basalts.
The formation of this basalt type is attributed to lava that predominantly degassed near or
at the vent during Hawaiian-style activity, producing far-traveled (hundreds of kilometers),
flat, and smooth-surfaced flows with low vesicularity that cooled into solidified basalts several tens
of meters thick. Such distal flows, often associated with sinuous rilles, are expected to extend
far from the eruption vent and form regolith protoliths consistent with the standard regolith
evolution model (Head et al., 2020). Our results therefore indicate that the CE5 and CE6 basalts
likely represent distal flows emplaced at considerable distance from their volcanic source vents.
In contrast, Apollo 15 basalt sample 15556 exhibits a void ratio of 13.6% (Gawronska et
al., 2022), representative of a vesicular basalt likely produced by inflated flows, highlighting
the clear distinction between these basalt types (Reply Figure 4b).

Response: Thanks for these constructive and insightful comments. Regarding the first point, we fully agree that investigating the relationship between vesicle abundance (represented by void ratio) and melt content is indeed meaningful, given that vesiculation is closely associated with agglutinitic melts. As we explained in our response to Comment #25, melt content is also related to fragment content (Fr). Therefore, here we focus on examining the relationship between the void ratio of larger agglutinates and their Fr. Based on statistical measurements from 43 CE5 and 43 CE6 larger agglutinates, we constructed the correlation shown in Reply Figure 5a. The results indicate that no clear relationship exists between void ratio and Fr. This may be because, although vesiculation is associated with agglutinitic melt, void ratio only partially reflects melt content. Vesicles can also form in inter-fragment void spaces or at the junctions between glass matrix and fragments during agglutinate formation, which decouples void ratio from melt content. Consequently, no inverse relationship between void ratio and Fr is observed.
To the reviewer’s second point, we appreciate the opportunity to clarify a potential misunderstanding. The observed difference in Ir values of bulk soil agglutinates between CE5 and CE6 is attributed to differences in the initial internal structures of larger agglutinates, rather than to additional processing experienced by the CE5 soils. Specifically, the larger CE5 agglutinates contain higher vesicularity, whereas CE6 agglutinates exhibit smaller vesicles and lower overall void ratio. These structural differences translate into subtle but statistically significant variations in the Ir values of their derived bulk soil agglutinates during subsequent space weathering. They do not imply that CE5 regolith underwent additional secondary agglutinate formation. The interpretation of the higher Ir in CE5 bulk soil agglutinates is explained in detail in our response to Comment #32.
In response to the reviewer’s suggestion, as other readers may also benefit from further clarification, we have added error bars for the CE5 and CE6 bulk soil agglutinate Ir and void ratio mean values in Figure 3a. (For Figure 3b, which shows individual data points, error bars are unnecessary.) Response: Very valuable comment. We agree that in our initial discussion we overstated the role of fragmentation in shaping particle morphologies within the bulk soil fraction, and we now recognize that the dominant regime in this size range is better described by a combination of mixing and agglutinate production.
In the revised manuscript, we have reorganized our discussion of particle reshaping mechanisms to capture the full spectrum of processes acting on lunar regolith. Specifically, include the following.
 Impact gardening (including mixing; primarily abrasion caused by repeated interactions among numerous grains within the regolith matrix)
 Impact fragmentation (grain breakage via direct energy deposition during impacts);
 Impact agglutination (fusion of surrounding grains into breccias or agglutinates due to impact-induced melts or semi-plastic phases)
 Impact sputtering (deposits from impact events appearing randomly on the surface of minerals, forming a sputtering deposit layer that modifies particle morphology)
 Impact abrasion (localized surface wear caused by micrometeoroid strikes or secondary impacts that generate linear scratches)
 Thermal fatigue (fracturing and disintegration from diurnal thermal stresses)
 Solar wind irradiation (implantation of high-energy ions producing lattice defects, which increase susceptibility to subsequent weathering-induced reshaping; in addition, sputtering by the solar wind which may also erode particle surfaces)
Among these, impact agglutination is particularly distinctive as it transforms “simple particles” into “complex particles” in a cumulative fashion, generating irregular aggregates that strongly influence bulk regolith morphology. By contrast, other processes reshape particles without fundamentally altering their type, although “complex particles” may shed small fragments that revert to “simple particles.” Both particle classes are then subject to additional modification by the full suite of processes.
Regarding the relative influence of fragmentation and abrasion, previous studies demonstrate that surface exposure age correlates with the grain size of lunar regolith in the >1 mm fraction (Morris, 1976; McKay et al., 1974), but this correlation weakens at <1 mm. Furthermore, Weibull fracture statistics demonstrate that smaller grains require higher stresses to fail completely (Weibull, 1951; McDowell et al., 2000). Thus, for the <1 mm grains that dominate the lunar regolith, impact fragmentation likely contributes only minimally to reshaping, and most of the impact energy is redistributed into broad-scale impact gardening, which thus emerges as the dominant driver of morphological modification (Reply Figure 6).
Despite clear differences in age, geological setting, basalt provenance, micrometeoroid flux, and solar wind irradiation between the CE5 and CE6 sampling sites, the morphometrics of corresponding particle types remain remarkably consistent. This convergence strongly suggests that long-term particle reshaping, governed primarily by impact gardening with contributions from agglutination, has driven both simple and complex particles toward stable morphologies, such that additional weathering exerts only a minor influence on their morphometrics.
Finally, we also fully agree with the reviewer that a more robust assessment of regolith maturity requires integrating multiple indicators. Accordingly, we now describe space weathering intensity using a multi-proxy suite of maturity parameters, including agglutinate abundance, Is/FeO values, and regolith surface exposure ages. For example, CE5 soils contain ~8% agglutinates, exhibit an Is/FeO value of ~14, and an exposure age of ~1.5 Ma (Qian et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025), whereas CE6 soils contain ~17% agglutinates, exhibit an Is/FeO value of ~56.5, and an exposure age of ~2.1 Ma (Zhang et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025). These parameters collectively indicate that CE6 experienced stronger space weathering than CE5. The consistent morphometrics observed across both soils therefore imply that even the less weathered CE5 regolith had already reached morphological saturation by its exposure age of ~1.5 Ma. This conclusion is further supported by our comparison with Apollo 17 sample 73002 (see Response to Comment #29), which represents an even more mature regolith yet exhibits similarly stable morphologies.

Response: Thanks for this valuable comment. We acknowledge that paragraph [15] in the original manuscript contained several shortcomings. First, our initial references to Apollo 11 and Apollo 17 soils did not specify sampling locations, which could have led to misunderstanding. Second, as Reviewer #1 correctly notes, the use of fine particle content as an indicator of space weathering intensity is problematic. Inspired by this (see Response to Comment 1(1)), we revisited the literature and found that local factors, such as proximity to boulders or recent craters, exert a strong influence on grain size characteristics (King, 1977). Thus, fine particle content cannot reliably serve as a proxy for space weathering intensity. In response, we have revised paragraph [15] to focus instead on a comprehensive description of space weathering intensity in CE5 and CE6 soils (see Revision to Comment #28).
And as this reviewer (#2) further suggests, validation of the morphological saturation effect requires more specific comparison with Apollo soils. To this end, we have incorporated data from the Apollo 17 double-drive tube sample 73001/2, specifically the upper 20 cm section (73002). This sample, recovered from the Light Mantle landslide deposit at the base of the South Massif in Taurus–Littrow Valley, was opened and scanned by micro-CT in 2019, with data subsequently released (Eckley et al., 2025). Previous work indicates that 73002 sampled multiple basalt flows, and its maturity is well constrained: the uppermost regolith exhibits an Is/FeO value of ~74 (Morris et al., 2022) and a surface exposure age of ~3.0 Ma (McFadden et al., 2024). By comparison, CE5 soils have an Is/FeO value of ~14 and an exposure age of ~1.5 Ma (Qian et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025), while CE6 soils show an Is/FeO of ~56.5 and an exposure age of ~2.1 Ma (Zhang et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025). Thus, the Apollo 17 sample is more mature than both CE5 and CE6, and its derivation from a landslide deposit ensures mineralogical and lithological complexity. If morphological saturation is also observed in 73002, this would imply that such saturation can be achieved by the relatively short exposure age of CE5 (~1.5 Ma).

33. Line 387-388: How does gardening, thermal cycling, and solar wind irradiation lead to
particle abrasion and fragmentation?
Response: Thanks for raising this important issue. We acknowledge that in the original version
our explanation of how gardening, thermal cycling, and solar wind irradiation contribute to
particle abrasion and fragmentation was not sufficiently clear, which may have led to confusion.
First, impact gardening is one of the dominant mechanisms reshaping lunar regolith
particles in our model (see Response to Comment #28-29). Within a given region, large
numbers of particles repeatedly make contact and undergo displacement, which results
predominantly in mechanical abrasion. (Tsuchiyama et al., 2022). For particles with structural
weaknesses—such as agglutinates containing abundant vesicles—gardening-induced
compression and stress concentration may also cause partial breakage.
Second, long-term thermal cycling, driven by daily non-uniform solar heating, induces
internal thermal stresses within particles. Over time, these stresses accumulate and may lead to
thermal fatigue, generating cracks that ultimately cause the particles to fracture (Ruesch et al.,
2020).
Finally, solar wind irradiation exerts its influence primarily in an indirect manner. The
implantation of high-energy ions generates crystalline defects that weaken lattice stability,
thereby making grains more susceptible to subsequent reshaping by other space weathering
processes (Maurette et al., 1975). In addition, sputtering by the solar wind which may also erode
particle surfaces (Tsuchiyama et al., 2022).
Together, these processes act in combination, progressively modifying particle
morphologies through abrasion and fragmentation.

impact abrasion (localized surface wear induced by micrometeoroid impacts20,91 or secondary

leading to ultimate grain disintegration90), and solar wind irradiation93 (high-energy ion
implantation generates crystalline defects, making grains more susceptible to subsequent space
weathering induced reshaping94; in addition, sputtering by solar wind may also erode particle
surfaces67).”

### Reviewer 1

The response letter provided very courteous and detailed explanations. In particular,
•A comparison with the Apollo samples has been added effectively.
•Analysis results for larger particles have been included.
•The term "dynamic equilibrium" has been removed.
•The evolutionary model of the lunar regolith has been improved.
•The connections with the referenced literature have become clearer.
•Overall, the accuracy of the descriptions has greatly increased.
As a result, the reviewer concluded that the manuscript is now suitable for publication in Nature Communication.

### Reviewer 2

We thank the authors for addressing our comments. From this, I see an immense improvement. This is demonstrated by a more robust literature review, which has helped guide the authors towards better interpretations of the data. However, there are still some outstanding clarifications and suggestions that I feel should be addressed before publication.
Paragraph 2:
According to the authors citations, the authors subdivisions for regolith particle sizes are based on simulant studies. How do these studies tie to natural regolith samples, other than their development to broadly mimic regolith composition? For example, the authors said that these divisions are based on different degrees of space weathering. Could the authors explain how these studies made this determination? I feel like a more robust description of this is warranted because to many researchers, anything <1 mm would be considered “dust” and described as “bulk soil”. If these classifications are the authors preference for the purposes of this work, I would make that clear in the text.
In addition, the observation of 20-200 um size fraction being more abundant than the “large” and “lunar dust” size fractions is in agreement with McKay et al 1974. It would be good to cite that here and elaborate why this phenomenon occurs when one would expect comminution to make smaller size fractions the most dominant.
Paragraph 5:
I would note here that regolith composition influences agglutinate abundance due to some mineral phases being more prone to melting. I recommend reviewing Adams and Charette, 1975: Chemical Fractionation of the Lunar Regolith by Impact Melting; Rhodes et al., 1975: Chemistry of Agglutinate Fractions in Lunar Soils.
Figure 2 appears to be blurry.
Supplementary Figure 2o: Nice work adding the extra data points. For stylistic purposes, each point is very similar in color, with Pyroxene and Olivene points being very close to the shaded region of Mp. Is it possible to change the color scheme of the figure so that the points for each mineral type are more easily distinguishable?
Paragraph 10:
Line 196-198: Solar wind contributes to npFe production embedded within agglutinates after exposure to kinetic energies associated from micrometeorite impacts. However, the glassy matrix is caused by impact melt, and solar wind is not a contributing factor. I would rephrase this to omit solar wind as an originating component to agglutinate formation and clarify that H from solar wind implantation into surface exposed regolith reduces iron in impact melt to form metallic iron nanoparticles (npFe) within agglutinitic glass. In addition, I would also elaborate on the proposed mechanisms that form vesicles within agglutinates.
Line 200-201: The phrasing of this sentence seems awkward. I recommend splitting these into two sentences, and introduce the influence of npFe when it is first introduced in the previous sentence.
I would also clarify what additional space weathering processes produce npFe, other than vapor deposition.
Paragraph 11:
Has the differences of vesicle morphology between glassy interiors and fragment interfaces been observed elsewhere using other methods?
Basu and McKay, 1985 conducted EDX analyses of the interfaces between agglutinitic melt and incorporated fragments and found no evidence of chemical gradation, suggesting that the two components don’t chemically influence each other. The authors results suggest that the interfaces influence vesicle morphology. Could the authors explain why this phenomenon occurs?
Additionally, do interfaces include older incorporated agglutinates? How can these agglutinate fragments be differentiated from lithic fragments in the authors CT data? How is this reconciled in the authors vesicle ratio calculations?
I am also curious how the authors define abundance of internal fragments. Is it a volumetric abundance? Numerical abundance? This is an important distinction as a particular Ir ratio may indicate one large fragment or multiple small fragments.
Paragraph 12:
I recommend removing the introduction of differences in micrometeorite bombardment and volatile mobilization as those are more relevant to the discussion.
The authors mention that the greater Ir values for bulk soils may be due to the inherent morphologies of fragmented larger agglutinates. Could it also be that bulk soil agglutinates form from smaller volumes of melt relative to the larger size fraction, and therefore would incorporate fewer fragments?
Paragraph 15:
Line 303-304: Agglutinate abundance is only a valid proxy for maturity for Is/FeO < 60. Agglutinate abundance saturates in more mature soils (Morris, 1976).
Line 306: I would say bombardment rather than vaporization, because npFe is found in melt AND vapor.
Line 307-310: Could the authors elaborate as to how regolith gardening manifests itself as exposure age? How is this age determined? The authors reference a paper that uses SEP tracks to identify exposure ages, however, for a given soil there ages can span millions of years while the average may only be only a fraction of the maximum age. The maximum age, therefore, may be a more appropriate metric to gauge the overall exposure age of a soil, since that is closer to the full duration that regolith had been exposed to space weathering processes. Are the ages the authors used for the Chang’e 5/6 samples the maximum age?
Paragraph 18
