Response: Thanks for this valuable comment. We acknowledge that paragraph [15] in the original manuscript contained several shortcomings. First, our initial references to Apollo 11 and Apollo 17 soils did not specify sampling locations, which could have led to misunderstanding. Second, as Reviewer #1 correctly notes, the use of fine particle content as an indicator of space weathering intensity is problematic. Inspired by this (see Response to Comment 1(1)), we revisited the literature and found that local factors, such as proximity to boulders or recent craters, exert a strong influence on grain size characteristics (King, 1977). Thus, fine particle content cannot reliably serve as a proxy for space weathering intensity. In response, we have revised paragraph [15] to focus instead on a comprehensive description of space weathering intensity in CE5 and CE6 soils (see Revision to Comment #28).
And as this reviewer (#2) further suggests, validation of the morphological saturation effect requires more specific comparison with Apollo soils. To this end, we have incorporated data from the Apollo 17 double-drive tube sample 73001/2, specifically the upper 20 cm section (73002). This sample, recovered from the Light Mantle landslide deposit at the base of the South Massif in Taurus–Littrow Valley, was opened and scanned by micro-CT in 2019, with data subsequently released (Eckley et al., 2025). Previous work indicates that 73002 sampled multiple basalt flows, and its maturity is well constrained: the uppermost regolith exhibits an Is/FeO value of ~74 (Morris et al., 2022) and a surface exposure age of ~3.0 Ma (McFadden et al., 2024). By comparison, CE5 soils have an Is/FeO value of ~14 and an exposure age of ~1.5 Ma (Qian et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025), while CE6 soils show an Is/FeO of ~56.5 and an exposure age of ~2.1 Ma (Zhang et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025). Thus, the Apollo 17 sample is more mature than both CE5 and CE6, and its derivation from a landslide deposit ensures mineralogical and lithological complexity. If morphological saturation is also observed in 73002, this would imply that such saturation can be achieved by the relatively short exposure age of CE5 (~1.5 Ma).
It should be noted, however, that the Apollo 73002 CT radiographs were acquired at a resolution of 25.8 μm (Eckley et al., 2025; Reply Fig. 7a), which limits morphological characterization to particles larger than ~500 μm. This precludes direct comparison with the bulk soil fraction (20–200 μm) analyzed in this study. To enable robust comparison, we therefore selected basalt particles in the 500–700 μm range from both CE5 and CE6 soils, using basalt as the common material for analysis (see Response to Reviewer#1 Comment 1(2)).
For CE5 and CE6, which are shallow scoop samples with relatively few large particles, we manually selected ~200 particles for each, from which we obtained 22 basalts from CE5 and 27 from CE6. For Apollo 73002, we restricted our analysis to the uppermost ~3 cm of regolith (to align with the near-surface context of CE5 and CE6 and to ensure comparable space weathering intensity). Basalt grains were readily identified from radiographs (Reply Fig. 7b), manually extracted, and reconstructed in 3D (Reply Fig. 7c–d). The larger sample size of Apollo 73002 allowed us to extract 110 basalt grains, ensuring statistical robustness.
Our morphometric results (Reply Fig. 7e–h) show highly similar distributions of AR, S, Cx, and R across basalts from CE5, CE6, and Apollo 17 (73002). The mean values differ by <10%, with comparable standard deviations. These results indicate that morphological saturation is likely already established by the CE5 surface exposure age of ~1.5 Ma, although larger CE5 and CE6 datasets will be necessary to further test this conclusion in the future.

have reached a saturation state in the youngest, least weathered CE5 regolith46, with the onset
of saturation thus occurring before ~1.5 Ma. To further test this striking hypothesis, we
examined Apollo 17 sample 73002, collected from the upper ~20 cm of the Light Mantle
landslide deposit at the base of the South Massif in the Taurus-Littrow Valley, a site at the mare-
highland boundary containing basalts of multiple ages88. The <1 mm fraction of this soil
exhibits an Is/FeO value of ~74 (ref. 101) and a surface exposure age of ~3.0 Ma (ref. 73),
indicating a higher degree of space weathering than either CE5 or CE6 soils. To verify whether
the same saturation trend holds for larger particles, we focused on mare basalts, the dominant
regolith component. We selected 22 basalt particles (500–700 µm) from CE5, 27 particles of
the same size range from CE6, and 110 particles from the upper 3 cm of Apollo 17 sample
73002 radiographs88. CE5 and CE6 basalts were analyzed using micro-CT scans at a voxel size
of 25.8 µm, the same resolution as applied to the 73002 radiographs. Morphometric results
show that even for larger particles in more strongly weathered soils, the saturation state may
persist (Supplementary Fig. 9), although further validation with larger datasets will be required.
During space weathering, regolith particles undergo repeated reshaping that ultimately leads to
progressive soil comminution. Larger particles are continually broken down into the bulk soil
fraction, while the bulk soil fraction itself steadily generates lunar dust. This process results in
the gradual enrichment of lunar dust within the regolith (Fig. 5).”

30. Line 357-370: Reference that discusses the latitudinal and longitudinal influence on
micrometeoroid impact: Sim et al. 2017: Asymmetric space weathering on lunar crater walls.
There are also plenty of other studies that model the flux of micrometeoroids on the lunar
surface.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this valuable comment. We acknowledge that our
manuscript did not originally address the latitudinal and longitudinal influence on
micrometeoroid flux. After carefully reviewing Sim et al. (2017), we note that micrometeoroid
flux is indeed latitude-dependent. This observation is consistent with the lunar surface flux
model of Jeong et al. (2015), which shows reduced flux at higher latitudes but remains
symmetric with respect to latitude. Since the CE5 and CE6 sampling sites are located at
43.06°N and 41.625°S in opposite hemispheres, respectively, their latitudes are nearly identical
(as designed by orbital mission planning requirements), suggesting comparable fluxes under
the similar longitudinal conditions.
In theory, the nearside may experience partial shielding by the Earth, potentially resulting
in a higher flux on the farside. However, Cremonese et al. (2013) quantified the “Earth
shielding effect” and found it to be on the order of 10-3, which is negligible. Their model also
indicates no significant longitudinal asymmetry in micrometeoroid flux. Taken together, these
results suggest that the CE5 and CE6 sites should experience broadly similar micrometeoroid
fluxes. We would like to emphasize that this inference is based on existing theoretical
frameworks and still requires more solid evidence from lunar regolith samples to be fully
validated by future work.
Revision: We have revised lines 380-384 to clarify our reasoning that CE5 and CE6 regions
are expected to experience comparable micrometeoroid fluxes. We now explicitly state that the
distinct internal structures observed between CE5 and CE6 agglutinates likely reflect regionally
distinct micrometeoroid bombardment intensities.
“Based on existing theoretical models, given the absence of hemispheric asymmetry in
micrometeorite flux at the lunar surface81 and the nearly identical absolute latitudes of the CE5
and CE6 sampling sites, the micrometeorite fluxes at the two regions are expected to be highly
similar81,82. Therefore, the notably distinct internal structures observed between CE5 and CE6
agglutinates likely reflect regionally different micrometeorite bombardment intensities.”

33. Line 387-388: How does gardening, thermal cycling, and solar wind irradiation lead to
particle abrasion and fragmentation?
Response: Thanks for raising this important issue. We acknowledge that in the original version
our explanation of how gardening, thermal cycling, and solar wind irradiation contribute to
particle abrasion and fragmentation was not sufficiently clear, which may have led to confusion.
First, impact gardening is one of the dominant mechanisms reshaping lunar regolith
particles in our model (see Response to Comment #28-29). Within a given region, large
numbers of particles repeatedly make contact and undergo displacement, which results
predominantly in mechanical abrasion. (Tsuchiyama et al., 2022). For particles with structural
weaknesses—such as agglutinates containing abundant vesicles—gardening-induced
compression and stress concentration may also cause partial breakage.
Second, long-term thermal cycling, driven by daily non-uniform solar heating, induces
internal thermal stresses within particles. Over time, these stresses accumulate and may lead to
thermal fatigue, generating cracks that ultimately cause the particles to fracture (Ruesch et al.,
2020).
Finally, solar wind irradiation exerts its influence primarily in an indirect manner. The
implantation of high-energy ions generates crystalline defects that weaken lattice stability,
thereby making grains more susceptible to subsequent reshaping by other space weathering
processes (Maurette et al., 1975). In addition, sputtering by the solar wind which may also erode
particle surfaces (Tsuchiyama et al., 2022).
Together, these processes act in combination, progressively modifying particle
morphologies through abrasion and fragmentation.
Revision: We have revised lines 420-430 to provide a clearer and more concise explanation of
how impact gardening, thermal cycling, and solar wind irradiation contribute to particle
abrasion and fragmentation.
“Particle reshaping processes at the lunar surface include impact gardening (mainly abrasion
caused by interactions among large numbers of particles within a given region78), impact
fragmentation (grain breakage due to direct energy deposition during impacts90), impact
agglutination (where impact-induced melts or semi-plastic phases fuse surrounding grains into
agglutinates and breccias), impact sputtering (deposits from impact events appear randomly on
the surface of minerals, forming sputtering deposit layer that modify particle morphology46),
impact abrasion (localized surface wear induced by micrometeoroid impacts20,91 or secondary
impacts that generate linear scratches92), thermal fatigue (fracturing driven by thermal stresses
leading to ultimate grain disintegration90), and solar wind irradiation93 (high-energy ion
implantation generates crystalline defects, making grains more susceptible to subsequent space
weathering induced reshaping94; in addition, sputtering by solar wind may also erode particle
surfaces67).”
